speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DREW  REFERENCE TO C.B.C. BROADCAST "CAPITAL REPORT"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to state a question of privilege affecting every hon. member of this house. It is in connection with a C.B.C. broadcast yesterday from Ottawa called "Capital Report". I have in my hand a copy of the text submitted to the station by Mr. Michael Barkway and I shall read the portion which I am making the subject of privilege. I think what I have to put forward constitutes one of the most astonishing breaches of the privileges, rights and responsibilities of the members of this house which can have come to the attention of any hon. member. I propose to read part of page 1 and page 2 of the text used yesterday by Mr. Barkway in the broadcast on a national network from Ottawa. After referring to what he described as the domestic drama of the Currie report, he went on to say:
As a drama critic, I think one's bound to say that act II wasn't up to the standard of excitement of act I. For one thing the sub-plot took up a disproportionate amount of attention. This is the mystery-now being cleared up-of how the C.C.F. party got its hands on an earlier draft of the report which Mr. Currie had neither approved nor signed. The first half of the answer is that the copy was stolen from a print shop in Montreal; and the man accused of stealing it is now in custody awaiting trial. How it got from the thief to Mr. Coldwell-who is certainly honest-we still don't know. But I suppose part of the scene of act III will be laid in a courtroom in Montreal, where some more of the story will come out.
The other part of act II which has now concluded was laid in parliament. I remember remarking on this program six weeks ago that Mr. Currie's description of the Petawawa horses on the pay roll was "more picturesque than precise". It turns out, in fact, to have been so imprecise as to have been false. It was taken, apparently, from the police records and the records of the Petawawa trials and in the process of condensation into one sentence it was wholly distorted. A cub reporter who had done the same thing would have lost his job.
You may think this was just by the way. But these inaccuracies in the Currie report-the horses and the false accusation that the C.N.R. let its tracks be stolen-I think they had a good deal to do with the major theme of the recent parliamentary debates. And that was whether the Currie report should be referred to the defence expenditures committee, or whether instead Mr. Currie
should be invited to extend his inquiries into the rest of the Department of National Defence. The government wanted to send the report to the commons committee for a fuller examination. The government majority-inevitably-voted to do that, and the committee has been set up. This wasn't what the opposition wanted. They say-and they're right-that the committee has a majority of Liberal members; and it's a foregone conclusion that its report will be as favourable to the government as the loyal Liberal majority can make it.
No doubt this is perfectly true. But the committee's report won't matter so much as the evidence which the committee hears-particularly from Mr. Currie himself. The inaccuracies of the original report-which are after all purely incidental-won't matter much if Mr. Currie has a mass of further detail to back up his charges of the "general breakdown in administration". But if he hasn't more detail than he gives in his report, then the government will be in a better position to claim that this is a bit of a storm in a teacup.
The most serious breach of the privileges, rights and responsibilities of members, Mr. Speaker, is the bald statement by this man who purports to be an accurate reporter-

I think it is our concern in this house to maintain responsibility for members of the press gallery who are part of the general proceedings of this house.

Privilege-Mr. Drew
Now, first of all, may I point to the fact that we have here the bald and emphatic statement, without any reservation, that the Currie report turns out in fact to have been so imprecise as to have been false. Mr. Speaker, I would have hoped that some member of the government would have risen to deal with a statement of that kind with regard to a man they had chosen, and whom they describe, as the most highly qualified man in the Dominion of Canada for the task allotted to him. Nevertheless, whether that might be regarded as the duty of the government or not, the fact remains, as very well might be pointed out, that such a statement is in itself wholly removed from the truth. No such finding has been made; and no such finding could be made.
May I also point out that we have this statement not only going out from this reporter but going out from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is guided by the policy laid down by the government, as stated by the minister responsible for that department.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On Friday, January 23, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) asked a question about a report in the newspapers concerning the purchase by the United Kingdom government of some 22 million bushels of wheat from Russia. I made a reply in general terms and promised to make an inquiry to get something more precise to put before the house. This is the information I have now obtained.
It is pointed out, in the first place, that the press reports of the negotiations refer to a quantity of 600,000 tons. I was not able at once to reduce that quantity into bushels, but I am told it is approximately the equivalent of 22 million bushels. In the second place, the report referred not only to wheat but to all grains, and particularly coarse grains. Hon. members will know that the United Kingdom has bought substantial quantities of coarse grains from Russia in the past few years, and the present negotiations are no doubt a continuation of that pattern. The quantities under negotiation, if correctly reported, would appear to be less than in previous years. Generally speaking, the United Kingdom has followed the practice of buying a large part of her wheat requirements in Canada, and the bulk of her coarse grain supplies elsewhere. In the first ten months of 1952, Canada exported only 1,615,000 bushels of barley to the United Kingdom.
On Friday I made reference to current negotiations between the United Kingdom and the Canadian wheat board. As a result of these negotiations, arrangements have been made for the United Kingdom ministry of food to take a portion of the agreed quantity of food for the present year-a rather small percentage-on a class II basis and price rather than under the lower international wheat agreement price. This arrangement will permit the United Kingdom to purchase under the international wheat agreement additional wheat which recently became available in Australia, and which it would otherwise have no right, under the international wheat agreement, to purchase at the class II price because Australia has been unable to fulfil the quota that it must dispose of under the international wheat agreement price. This arrangement does not,

Questions
however, up to the present time, involve any change in the quantity of 115 million bushels which was announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) as the amount which the United Kingdom had contracted to purchase. It may mean that for a certain portion of it the wheat board will be getting a somewhat higher price than under the original agreement.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think this motion might be adopted. As far as I have been able to ascertain, the only communications were between Mr. Nollet and myself. I now table the telegram I received from him and the answer I addressed to him on January 15.

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, I shall first of all anticipate the arguments of the opponents to the subject matter of this resolution by stating that we in this party would wish-and in fact would insist-that such federal aid as that visualized in the terms of the resolution should in no way involve any interference with provincial jurisdiction over education. Such aid as I visualize would be simply an extension of the extensive aid which is now rendered by the dominion government to education in the provinces and which has been such a distinct benefit to the provinces and indeed to the nation. This aid has been received by all the provinces of Canada, including those which have been most insistent upon their retention of provincial rights. Nowhere has it been argued

and certainly not in this house-that the aid which has already been extended in that matter has in any way interfered with provincial jurisdiction over education, particularly in the vital matters of method, administration and curriculum. The aid to which I have referred has been extended with respect to vocational training, technical training, scholarships in research and the like. I shall refer only to those now, but I have in my hand a sessional paper which shows that vast amounts of money have been expended by the federal government in the provinces for education in other directions.
This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that I have propounded these arguments.
TMr. St. Laurent.]
For the sake of those who are actually interested in this matter and would care to do some research on it, I would refer to the debate which took place the last time I moved this resolution, namely on March 19, 1952, at which time the debate continued on March 20. Today, instead of bringing forth those rather academic arguments-I think they were once so characterized by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); I have brought them forward year after year and the house must be familiar with them all-I want to deal rather with the effect which this resolution is having upon the opinions of the people in the country with regard to it. When I shall have finished, Mr. Speaker, I think you will decide that I have support in some rather unexpected quarters.
At any rate, in my speech on the date that I have mentioned, I dealt with 1he alarming situation in education which has developed in Canada. The last time I moved this resolution it was talked out by a Liberal member of this house. The speech itself which opened the debate dealt largely with the shortage of teachers, the dropping off in the number of students enrolling in the teaching profession, and the great increase in the enrolment in both elementary and secondary schools. At the time of the debate I presented figures to substantiate my arguments in those directions. Those figures I obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics and other reliable sources. These things are of interest surely to all Canadians. I confess that my own interest in the matter is the welfare of all Canadian children, and I lay the emphasis upon the "all". As reported at page 590 of Hansard of March 19, 1952, I stated:
The principle behind the resolution is that all children in Canada should enjoy equality of opportunity of education irrespective of their geographical position, of the country of origin of their parents, or of their economic status. That should be denied to no child in Canada, irrespective of where he may live and irrespective of his origin.
My aim is a degree of equality of educational opportunity for all Canadian children. May I say to one or two of my friends who need to be told, that I have no desire to ask for uniformity in education or equality of education; I am asking for equality of opportunity in education, which is a vastly different thing.
In the speech, the date of which I have mentioned, I produced evidence of glaring inequalities of opportunity in education all across this country. That inequality is due to the difference in the ability of the provinces to raise funds for educational purposes. In the particular tables of figures

from the dominion bureau of statistics which I quoted at page 591 of Hansard in that debate in regard to the amount spent per child by the various provinces upon education, I find that the expenditure per pupil on public, elementary and secondary education on an average daily attendance basis in 1949 is as follows: British Columbia spent $244; Alberta spent $201; Saskatchewan, $174. These are the three highest, as compared with the three lowest Newfoundland, $77; Prince Edward Island, $83; and Nova Scotia, $114. My hon. friends will agree with me that there is not much equality of opportunity depicted in these particular figures.
Many children are having to put up with unqualified teachers and, worse still, with persons who are sitting in a chair presiding over the school and who are not teachers at all.
An interesting pamphlet has been published lately, I think in preparation for education week, by the Canadian education week national headquarters at Ottawa. It says this:
The teacher is the most important single factor in the success or failure of our educational system. Canada needs to have more of her best young people enter this profession. We should be concerned about retainment as well as recruitment. We can help by supporting measures that will elevate the prestige of this profession. Better teacher education, better salaries, improved working and living conditions are essential.
We cannot have good teachers unless we are prepared to provide the above conditions. At the time of the debate last year it was estimated that the teacher shortage-and this is serious-by 1955 would have climbed to 2,500, and at the same time the normal school enrolment had dropped by 20 per cent in a single year. The pamphlet also mentions as well as the teacher shortage another imminent problem, and that is the increasing pupil enrolment. I shall quote that part of the pamphlet. It says this:
The swelling flood of school enrolments, having filled our elementary grades to the bursting point in the immediate post-war period, is now about to descend on the higher grades and secondary schools. We must be ready for this influx or our crowded schools will be literally swamped and the teacher shortage, already serious, will become critical.
In this pamphlet there is a chart. I shall not quote the passage, but I shall give the figures of the estimates of secondary school enrolment in the years from 1952 to 1964. They have given 1952 figures of 300,000 children enrolled in the secondary schools, and the estimated figure for 1964 is 620,000, or a secondary school enrolment which will double itself in the next twelve years. I
Education
ask you, sir, whether or not under our present conditions of education in the provinces, and particularly in some of the provinces, we are now equipped to deal with that condition. It is an interesting thing, and I think it is based on the province of Ontario, to look at the commentary by Francis Oakes Baldwin of Ottawa. This commentator quotes J. T. Stubbs, president of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation, as follows:
J. T. Stubbs made it clear that the present shortage is just a taste of what is to come-and he made it clear that he was not speaking only of Ontario. He said: "We are resting in a momentary calm at the heart of an educational hurricane-the most alarming teacher shortage ever to face the secondary schools of this province.
I shall not continue to read it, but it goes on to give the figures on the elementary schools and the increases therein. He calls it the swollen attendance in our public schools.
Now, sir, I suppose it is a condition of our history that most of the aid which has been given by this government to education in this country has been extended in a rather underhand and furtive manner. I would suggest that if the government is not prepared to accept this resolution-and I have no doubts about that particular matter-then there are one or two ways in which it might continue this furtive aid to education without making it, as it appears to be today, a political issue. I am thinking of one or two things; I am thinking of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, for example, where we have great numbers of people coming into this country from other countries and bringing their children with them. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration, without saying too much about it, has had to bolster the finances of suburban parts of cities and towns, mining camps and so on, so that schools may be built for the children of those new citizens. I suggest that that is the way that the government could continue to do this thing which it is not supposed to do. In a matter of teachers' training, I would suggest that if we are to get enough teachers in the immediate future we shall have to do something, and I would suggest that the government might even try something which they could very well do without having any suspicion or even an argument raised against interference with provincial autonomy in that field. The teachers' training would still remain in the hands of the provincial authorities themselves and the federal government could stand by with a little financial aid.
I could go on and say a word or two about the same sort of thing in the Department of National Health and Welfare, but I want

Education
to leave that phase of the question for a moment. As I have said, federal aid to education has already been very general and very generous in spots, and I think almost wholly successful. There is a long list of things in which the government has taken part. As a matter of fact, the federal government is up to its neck in aid to education now. I hold in my hand sessional paper 184, tabled in the House of Commons on May 2, 1952, which shows that millions of dollars have been spent. The list is too lengthy to read. There is apprenticeship training; youth training; supervisory training; training of persons to fit them for the armed forces. That is a sad confession. They have to educate people in order to fit them for the armed forces; training of persons to fit them for gainful employment; vocational training for discharged members of the armed forces; vocational correspondence schools; payments to provinces for capital expenditures for education, and so forth; Indian education. There are dozens of places where millions of dollars are being spent at the present time for the purpose of education.
We have of course the recent payment, and the thing which perhaps I am most thankful of all for, namely, the present aid to the universities of Canada, without which aid I see no other alternative but a breakdown in our higher education in the universities of Canada. I hear there is some talk of further expansion of scholarship grants and some federal aid to the children of veterans.
Well, sir, I am in favour of it, but I would suggest that what is good for the children of veterans is also good for other people's children.
Those who have supported the government in its stand have, for want of a better argument, resorted to what I believe is a false one, that the whole matter is unconstitutional. Again, I challenge anyone either in the house or outside of it to say that the grants I have listed have taken away, in any degree, any of the jurisdiction of the provinces over education. Neither has there been any actual interference by federal authorities either with the administration or with the curriculum of the schools.
In various places-seldom, it is true-I have been accused of raising this argument for some ulterior motive. It has been said that I have done so for purposes of political gain. Let me assure my hon. friends that I was working for federal aid for education long before I took an active part in politics, or ever saw this House of Commons.
Let me draw to the attention of the government and the house just how this issue of

federal aid to education is considered throughout the country. Up to this time I have tried to keep this matter from becoming a political issue, and I have placed on the records of the house all the non-political arguments I could bring to bear. I suggest now however that the subject is likely to become a political issue. I fancy it will be in my part of the country during the next election campaign; but if it is, I shall not accept responsibility for it.
I can show from files on my desk that the subject matter of this resolution has been favoured by branches of the I.O.D.E., Legion organizations, labour organizations, agricultural co-operatives, and the Canadian Trustees Association. This is a matter which is the concern of many people throughout the country.
The Canadian School Trustees Association has been particularly active. At the very moment I speak they are aiming to collect between $30,000 and $40,000 to be spent on research in this very matter. They have employed Dr. LaZerte, one-time dean of education in Alberta, to carry out research; and the Canadian Teachers Federation will of course support that project. I do not know whether they have subscribed financially to the campaign, but I believe they are going to institute a similar research program, if they do not join the Canadian School Trustees Association in the other one.
To support that point I should like to read from a pamphlet issued by the Canadian School Trustees Association. It bears the title "Federal Aid", is taken from the Canadian Teachers Federation news letter, and states:
The Canadian Teachers Federation will continue its campaign for education and in this connection will give financial support and actively co-operate with the Canadian School Trustees Association in their research project under the direction of Dr. M. E. LaZerte. This outstanding educationalist has accepted a two-year contract with the trustees to do a fact-finding survey of educational finance with particular reference to need for federal aid.
The fact of the matter is-and this is the most important thing I shall say today-that the expenses of education can no longer be borne by municipalities at the local level. These municipalities turn to their provinces for aid; and in that I wish them all success. I am in favour of educational aid from every source that it can be obtained. But some of the provinces are at the end of their financial tether. Local taxation upon real estate can no longer bear all the brunt. The basis of taxation for purposes of education must be broadened; and the federal government is the only institution of which I am aware

with the resources necessary to make possible the equalization of educational opportunities.
I say that federal aid is the only aid by which we will be able to lower the tax rate on local municipalities. This applies particularly to suburban municipalities, where there has been a great influx of new population, where there has been new building and there is a necessity for new schools. In that connection federal aid might well take the form of the payment of expenses in connection with the building of those institutions.
I could give dozens of examples. Here is one. Only yesterday I received a newspaper clipping-and I am sorry I cannot give the name of the publication although, from the appearance of it, it would seem to be an Ontario agricultural paper. It is headed "School Tax Protested at Federation Meeting". The federation to which reference is made is the Ontario federation of agriculture, before whom Mr. Heatherington made a report in which he said:
Because of the tremendous burden imposed on rural municipalities, due to the need for expansion of present educational facilities, we strongly suggest that the full capital cost of all new school buildings should be borne by the provincial and/or federal governments.
And at that meeting it is indicated that a Mr. Laventure said that he wanted action, "even if it meant a fight." I do not know with whom he was going to fight. At any rate this gentleman who lives in McNab township, county of Renfrew, said that his school tax alone was $185. Then the article goes on to say:
The average one hundred acre farm in his township paid $60 to $80 in school tax, while the village dwellers paid $6 to $8. Farm property pays 10 times as much school tax as non-farmers pay on their dwellings, he said.
I offer this as some evidence as to what people are thinking concerning the source to which they should turn for relief of this condition.
As I said a moment ago, I have tried to keep the discussion non-political, but have warned the government that it could and probably would become political. My submission is that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made it a political matter when, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who was requested by some of the local school people to support an application for federal aid for education-
Education

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Winnipeg school board.

-the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 1355 of Hansard for November 27, 1951:
While I have the responsibility as the head of the government I would have to ask my colleagues to join with me in refusing to consider such a request.
Then, I have referred to what I said on Friday, March 19, 1952, as reported at page 593:
I should like to warn this government, in terms that it understands, that in the past five years a tremendous demand for federal aid to education has been created.
And again, on the same page:
I warn the government that so far as we in western Canada are concerned, ninety per cent of the people who are represented by the Liberal members from Saskatchewan are in favour of federal aid to education. Up to the moment I have not heard much support .for that cause from those particular backbenchers.
When I said that I was talking about the backbenchers from Saskatchewan in the Liberal party. We are approaching a federal election, and the government should know that the people of this country in most places support the general terms of this resolution. It is fair to say that the party of which I am a part has supported it unanimously over the years, and I think the same can be said for the Social Credit party. With only a few reservations, where some doubts have been expressed about provincial autonomy it can be said, too, of the Conservative party. And the reservation in connection with provincial autonomy is a perfectly legitimate one; we are making it ourselves.
But I have found that our Liberal friends supporting the government, so far as their votes in the house, or their words in debate are concerned, have been diametrically opposed to it. I say this does become a political issue when the opposition to this measure comes from the Liberal benches, is led by the Prime Minister, and three outstanding ministers of the government, among whom is the one now looking in my direction, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). He and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) appear to be the men who were chosen to lead the opposition of their confreres against this resolution. So I state that it is somewhat of a political issue today. So far as the backbenchers are concerned, they of course voted against the resolution, having taken their cue from whatever minister happened to be leading the fight against it on the particular day. I have made statements that the people in my own province and the people of constituencies represented here by

Education
Liberal members are about 90 per cent in favour of the terms of this resolution. Naturally I have no statistics and cannot prove that opinion. Only one Liberal backbencher, the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison), actually spoke against the resolution and his speech is found at pages 644 and 645 of Hansard for March 20, 1952. In reply to my assertion with respect to the 90 per cent he said, as found at page 645:
I can say that I never had anyone mention to me federal aid for education.
That was his reply to my assertion that there was a lot of interest in the subject. Then he went on to say with respect to my figure of 90 per cent:
I would say that the only 90 per cent figure in that area I covered would be the number of those who are just plumb-
That is not my word. He said "plumb".
-against that provincial government. They are going to change it-and they are going to change it this summer.
I would suggest that if my hon. friend is no greater authority upon federal aid to education or education generally than he was a prognosticator of the results of that provincial election, then he does not know too much about it. My hon. friend of course did not debate the resolution at all. He simply loosed a wild tirade against the provincial government and, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that comes pretty ill from a member whose district has the highest equalization grant given by the province of Saskatchewan. In that whole federal constituency, as was later brought out by Mr. Lloyd, the minister of education, 72 per cent of the total cost of education in that member's entire territory is furnished today by the provincial government of Saskatchewan.
How?

I hear some murmurs from some of my backbench Liberal friends. They apparently like this so I will give them more of it. The remarks of the hon. member for Meadow Lake were deeply resented throughout the province and I bring this letter to the attention of the house to show what the people of the country really think about this resolution for federal aid to education. The Saskatchewan school trustees association sent the hon. member a letter which he said he would put upon Hansard. For some reason he neglected to do that. He rose on a question of privilege with respect to the letter on March 31, as found at page 944 of Hansard.
What year?

1952. The hon. member was interrupted in his remarks by the hon. mem-

ber for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) who asked the following question:
Would the hon. member put on the record the letter to which he Is referring?
The hon. member for Meadow Lake said, "I shall be pleased to do so", but somehow or other in the heat of argument he neglected to put the letter on the record, and therefore it is my intention to do it for him today. The letter had enclosed with it a resolution passed at the provincial executive meeting of the Saskatchewan school trustees association held in Saskatoon on March 22, 1952. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas from press reports it appears that Mr. J. H. Harrison, M.P., of Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan, when speaking in the House of Commons, stated that Saskatchewan had "the worst situation in education to be found anywhere in Canada" and further "the reason Saskatchewan had no teachers was that the larger school units-
I will leave out that part.
Read it all.
All right.

Saskatchewan spends less
money on education than any other province.

I continue:
-did the hiring and they did not go into the competitive market";
And whereas in our opinion-
These are the words of the resolution of the Saskatchewan school trustees' association, a non-political body.
-these statements are false and malicious and serve only to create a grave injustice to the teachers and school trustees of the province of Saskatchewan and to educational progress generally in our province.
And whereas it would appear from these statements that Mr. Harrison is ignorant of the true situation within the province of Saskatchewan and even of the situation in and benefits obtained by his home town of Meadow Lake.
Now therefore be it resolved that the secretary be instructed to write Mr. Harrison, forwarding a copy of this resolution and requesting him to withdraw his statement so made in the House of Commons and to apologize for the injustice thereby created to the end that the stigma which he has attached to those interested in education in our province, including teachers and school trustees individually and this association, be removed.
That resolution was carried unanimously and forwarded to every member of parliament representing a seat in the province of Saskatchewan. So much for my friend from Meadow Lake. I said that the matter was to some extent becoming a political issue, and I suggest that the hon. member helped to make it so when, in attempting to defend himself, he wrote a letter to an organization of teachers in his own territory who had asked for an explanation as to why he, their member, had opposed my resolution for federal aid to education. He wrote an amazing letter

which is worth a lot just as a source of amusement. My friend thought it was a good letter so he sent it to the North Battleford Optimist and the Turtleford Times. I should like every hon. member to listen to this. It shows the methods of these people. He said:
As a Liberal member here, Mr. Knight's resolution to me-
This is his explanation of why he voted against it.
-was nothing more nor less than a C.C.F. motion. It was put in there expressly to deceive people.
I challenge the Minister of Justice or anyone within the sound of my voice to suggest to me face to face in the house that I have moved this resolution deliberately for the purpose of deceiving people. That is the kind of thing we get on the hustings these days. Out west even Liberal constituents believe in federal aid to education but apparently the federal Liberal members of parliament do not. I want to relate another little incident. My very good and personal friend, the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), came to Saskatoon a little while ago and I suppose he thought he should say a word or two about his M.P. host while he was there. He met a body of Liberals, but I do not know whether it was the Saskatoon or Saskatchewan Liberal association. At any rate, he met some of them. My hon. friend was hardly fair in what he said because, according to the press report, he insinuated that I was prepared to accept federal control over education, something which the hon. member has heard me deny time and time again in this house, or else he has read it in Hansard if he has done me the honour to read my speeches. As an intelligent member of parliament, I expect that the same hon. gentleman has done me that honour.
He spoke in Saskatoon, and it is most amusing. I said I would show that there was support for this resolution in very curious places, so I am going to read a short extract from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix dealing with the meeting of the Liberal association held on October 9, 1952. It is as follows:
Another resolution dealing with federal aid to education also touched off warm debate and finally was passed in an innocuous form.
That "innocuous" is good.
A. G. Lamarsh originally urged that the meeting go on record as endorsing federal aid to education and said it was inevitable that it would come eventually.
Then the paper quotes him as saying:
I think we should be climbing aboard the bandwagon-
How like my Liberal friends.
-and taking some of the credit for it, and not let Mr. Knight (R. R. Knight, C.C.F., M.P. for Saskatoon) steal our thunder.
Education
"Our thunder". Whose thunder? It makes me think of Mr. Churchill's famous expression about "some chicken-some neck".
There was another gentleman present at this Liberal meeting who said:
It would be a catastrophe if the federal government ever came to a point where it controlled education.
It goes on:
Mr. Larson said he did not think even Saskatchewan wanted the federal government to take over education and there was already a good deal of criticism of the federal government for its taxation policies-
He felt that federal aid to higher forms of education, such as the national research council, was all right, but if it was granted to primary and secondary education it would cut across a lot of religious and other barriers. He added that he thought-
And this is significant.
*-Mr. Knight will run into a lot of trouble over the issue, and he has received very little support for his motion to date.
-in spite of these appeals and letters that I have had from organizations all over this country.
Then I will give you a typical Liberal resolution which comes at the end.
Mr. Lamarsh finally changed his resolution to one asking the executive to investigate the problem with a view to bringing in a future resolution if it was believed advisable.
Shades of Mr. Mackenzie King!
Liberals all.

Now, sir, I have finished but I would just like to put on the record, so we may know what we have been talking about, a paraphrase of a paragraph of my speech last year. I have put forward certain conclusions. Firstly, I have set forth as a matter of premise the democratic principle that every child in Canada should have as a right equal opportunity of education with every other child in Canada. Secondly, I have shown that the education system is riddled with inequalities and the cause of such inequalities is largely financial. Thirdly, I have shown that municipalities in certain provinces, and those provinces themselves, are unable to cope with the expenditure needed to bring about that equality.
Finally, asserting that such equality of opportunity is a subject of national concern, I urge that the dominion government, the only body with the necessary financial resources, while safeguarding the jurisdiction of the provinces over education within their own boundaries, should proceed forthwith to inaugurate a system of federal aid to education in Canada.
Here is a last paragraph, this time from my speech of May 22, 1950, which I would

Education
like to put on the record. This is not a wishy-washy innocuous resolution put because somebody thought it is necessary to get on the bandwagon. Here is what I said and by it I am prepared to stand or fall:
The birthright of every child is a minimum standard of education, based not on the wealth of the parent, of the local school district, or even of the province, but on the wealth and the resources of the whole country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Adjourn the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I am going to disappoint my hon. friends, for I am not going to adjourn the debate.
I am a little bit embarrassed, Mr. Speaker, as a minister, in rising so soon to take part in the debate on a resolution moved by a private member on the opposition side. I do so only because I have another engagement this afternoon which I made long before I had any idea that this subject would come up now. I must get away to attend if I possibly can.
I would like to compliment the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) on the presentation which he has just made, which I am sure from his standpoint at least is a fair one. With respect to some of the main points which he has made I do not think there will be any disagreement on the part of any member of this house. No one will disagree with the splendid rhetoric with which he closed his remarks to the effect that every Canadian child should have as far as possible equal opportunity of adequate education. But I would point out that in this matter in Canada, with the peculiar set-up we have, the means to these very desirable ends which he has enunciated is of very considerable importance. I would point out, moreover, that every competent body of specialists that I know of which has investigated this problem of the best method of providing adequate support for primary education has reached conclusions which are quite different from those which are pressed by my hon. friend.
Not the municipal experts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not necessarily the municipal experts. I am referring to the body which was set up to deal with this very problem in the 1930's when it was a much more acute problem than it is at the present time- the Rowell-Sirois commission set up in 1937. That was the latter part of the depression when the problem of providing a very much lower standard of expenditure for primary education was much more acute than it is for us now to provide a much higher expenditure. This was one of the main problems
fMr. Knight.]
with which the provinces, the municipalities and, as related to them, the federal government, were faced.
That body dealt specifically with this very question and made certain comments upon it to which I shall refer in due course. Following that there were conferences between the provinces and the dominion, which, after some ups and downs, eventually culminated in the present tax agreements between those two levels of government. Throughout all of those proceedings the desire and the objective was to place all of the provinces in a position where they would be able to discharge their constitutional responsibilities for, amongst other things, primary education-without any interference in the discretion they would exercise in discharging their responsibilities in their own field of jurisdiction.
The present financial arrangements between the dominion and the provinces-under the tax agreements-are the result of the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report to put into the hands of the provincial governments, from federal sources, grants of income which the provinces themselves can spend as they choose. Whether they wish to spend it for primary education or for the building of roads or for any other provincial function is their choice. In other words, the central purpose was to provide all of the provinces with financial means of discharging their responsibilities-leaving with the provinces the sole discretion of how they should do that. Whether they spend more money on primary education and less on roads and the like is entirely up to them.
It is in the light of these decisions and recommendations, recommendations by the Rowell-Sirois report and decisions reached between the provincial governments and the federal government, to which only the other day the province of Ontario subscribed, as the ninth province to do so, it is under these arrangements that the provinces are in a better position to make provision for primary education, among other things.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) was fair enough in his remarks to admit that the federal government gives large educational grants to the universities and training schools which are set up for specific purposes under the joint auspices of the federal and provincial governments. I am sure that he would be the first to admit that these arrangements represent the willingness of the federal government to make contributions to the provincial governments in all of those cases in which it is possible to do so without interfering in any way with the provinces' exclusive control over primary education

In support of what I have just been saying,
I should like to quote from the Rowell-Sirois report, because I do not know of any other place in which these principles are more lucidly set forth. I should like to quote from volume II of the report, page 50, to this effect: We have already said that the instruction of the young during their formative years is a matter which the provinces must continue to control (subject, of course, to the safeguard for religious minorities provided in the British North America Act and amendments). A free hand in something so important to the social and cultural life of the people seems to us to be vital to any provincial autonomy worthy of the name, and it is obvious that any attempts to alter the existing arrangements would meet with powerful opposition and would provoke profound resentment.
I suggest that the hon. member for Saskatoon, as a school teacher, must be assumed to be familiar with some Canadian history.
I hope he is. As a school teacher, and as a member of this house, I am sure he will not disagree with that principle enunciated in the Sirois report.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is quite obvious to anyone who stops to reflect upon this matter that it is one thing for the federal government to make grants, for example, to the universities which are self-governing and self-contained. They exercise their own discretion as to the manner in which those grants shall be spent. Any government, whether provincial or federal, knows that in making such grants to universities it has given up any kind of residual control that it might wish to exercise. To argue, because it is proper, in the light of Canadian history, to make grants to institutions of that kind, that it is equally proper to make grants to provincial governments earmarked for primary education, is a totally different matter. It is impossible to draw any proper analogy between the two types of grants.
This is indicated by a further comment from the Rowell-Sirois report. At page 51 they say:
Many representations have been made to us that financial help should be extended by the dominion to the provinces for various purposes, such as scholarships, technical training, grants to be used for general educational purposes provided that the provinces did not reduce their own expenditure on education. These representations appear to have been inspired largely by consternation-
Remember that this was back in the time when provincial expenditures for education were a great deal lower than they are now.
-at the reductions in educational expenditure which certain provinces, under the stress of the depression, have felt compelled to make. It has even been contended that the dominion is bound to see that there is equal educational opportunity (as far as is practicable) for every Canadian child. We have the deepest sympathy for these views which have been advanced by many of the organizations most closely associated with education in Canada, and we share to the full the regret that,
Education
especially in recent years, education has been terribly neglected in many of the poorer parts of the country and that wholly disproportionate sacrifices have been imposed on those who have devoted their lives to this important public service. But the representations appear to us to go too far in denying the right of each province to decide the relative importance of expenditure on education and expenditure on other competing services. It is our hope-
Now, they are enunciating here a principle which is one of the cardinal principles of the Rowell-Sirois report, which is one of the basic principles of the financial arrangements which have been reached between the federal government and the provinces, and which is the only principle upon which it is possible, in these financial arrangements, to have proper respect for provincial autonomy.

that provision can be made for the fiscal needs of all provinces, including within those needs provision for the education of the young. Our financial proposals aim at placing every province in a position to discharge its responsibilities for education (on a scale-
Now, this is an important consideration for my hon. friend to listen to. The taxpayers of this country will certainly listen to it.
-that is within the means of the people of Canada) if it chooses to do so.
If we say, as the motion does, that the federal government should make grants to the provinces to supplement their expenditures for primary education at the present time when their budgets are certainly in a very buoyant condition, if we say it is still necessary to supplement them at this time, and the proposal is-I am sure my hon. friend will agree with this-that sums which would reach large amounts should be paid to the provinces for that purpose and earmarked for primary education, no one with any practical knowledge of public administration would say that there was not a clear responsibility upon the federal government to exercise a reasonable degree of supervision to make sure that the moneys voted by parliament, allocated for purposes of that sort, are actually expended for the purposes for which they have been given to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Education
which makes the grant to build that school does satisfy itself that the school meets certain standards and that it is properly built. I would point out to my hon. friend that if he has any idea of Canadian history he will surely be able to distinguish between that case and the case of moneys turned over for the payment of teachers and the like in the field of primary education, involving continuous supervision of provincial expenditures over a period of years.
He would have to be a Liberal lawyer to make that distinction.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This money has been turned over to the Winnipeg school board.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Yes, turned over for the purpose of making a capital expenditure. If my hon. friend spoke with knowledge, he would be telling the house that there are careful checks made in all of these cases to ensure that the money is being properly spent. I do not think my hon. friend is taking the position that the Rowell-Sirois recommendations are wrong. I do not think he is taking the position in opposition to these tax agreements, because certainly if he did he would be acting very much against the interest of the province from which he comes. But what he is saying is that after these arrangements have been made, he is not satisfied as a teacher, as a member of the house or as a Canadian, if you like, with the amount of money which the provincial government, with all the grants which it receives, is spending for primary education in the province of Saskatchewan. That being the case, he wants the federal taxpayers to pay over some more money for that purpose.
There was a time, Mr. Speaker, when a case of that sort could be put up with a great deal more cogency and force than can be done at the present time. Back at the time when the Rowell-Sirois commission was set up, it was quite true that the amounts which were being spent for educational purposes were disgraceful, and that they were much more disgraceful than they are at the present time. My hon. friend may say that they are still disgraceful, even in the province of Saskatchewan. He may say that. But if they are, then may I say I have a few figures here to show that if the province of Saskatchewan wishes to do so it can certainly spend on primary education more money than it is at present spending-
May I interrupt-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me to finish my sentence, I shall be glad.
I was going on to say that the figures also show that the province of Saskatchewan has

been placed in a posiuoi. uo so by the very tax agreements whose adequacy my hon. friend is now challenging.
I say to him that the western provinces and the maritimes particularly-and other provinces of Canada; Ontario is now included -have worked extremely hard to find, under the existing distribution of responsibilities between the federal government and the provincial governments, seme method whereby every province in Canada, within reasonable limits, could provide at least a minimum service in the field of education and other fields of provincial responsibility; and they have, after long negotiations and much travail, finally obtained an arrangement which is working reasonably well. What I warn my hon. friend against is leaning too heavily on special earmarked grants and tearing down the whole structure of federal-provincial finance.
When we look at the facts, what do we find? We find that in 1939 the total expenditure on education in all of the provinces was $38 million. At that time-even then-the total expenditure upon highways and bridges was $87-6 million. But in 1949, after the tax agreements had been in effect but before they were signed by Ontario, the amount spent on education was over $154 million- up from $38 million-an increase of more than fourfold in ten years. But during that period of time the expenditures upon highways and bridges by the provinces had been enlarged by $164 million per year because, in part, of the assistance which they had obtained in these tax agreements. The total provincial expenditures in 1939 in all provinces were $356 million. In 1949 they were $858 million.
In the face of these facts, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me to be an extremely difficult thing for a member of this house-even such an eloquent gentleman as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight)-to say with any force that, in this increase in expenditures from $356 million to $858 million, there was no room or no adequate scope for a larger increase upon education if the provincial government charged with the constitutional responsibility for dealing with primary education had chosen or had desired to spend more money upon that function. In the face of this large over-all increase in all other forms of provincial expenditure, surely no one can suggest otherwise than that if the provision for education is as inadequate as the hon. gentleman suggests it is, then the provincial ministers have the clear responsibility, and not only this government but provincial governments, provincial public

men, the Sirois commission and those who took part in the discussions between the provinces and the dominion leading up to the tax agreements, all seemed to think that it was desirable that the provinces should continue to retain and to exercise that responsibility.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Surely.

Has he read the pronouncement of Premier Campbell of Manitoba in that regard at the time the provincial conference was being set up and also the request of Premier Douglas that this matter should form part of the agenda?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I shall be glad indeed to do that if I may make that interjection right :iow. As to Manitoba, for the information of

my hon. friend, although I am sure that he knows it quite well, under these tax agreements that province is getting-and I am just speaking from memory-about three times as much as it was able to get from those same revenue sources by provincial taxes which at that time were the highest of their kind on the North American continent. They are getting it without the imposition of those taxes and without the imposition of as high taxes as Saskatchewan has, with the imposition of only a nine-cent gasoline tax, with no sales tax of any kind at all, and have been able to increase their budget from something of the order of $17 million to between $40 million and $45 million.
Having made that comment upon Manitoba, may I be permitted to deal with Saskatchewan. In 1952-53, these are the amounts paid by the federal government into Saskatchewan: Subsidy, $24,626,000-that is under the tax agreement; health grants, $2 million; pensions to persons 65 to 69, $2,024,000; pensions for the blind, $155,000; vocational training, $128,000; trans-Canada highway, $1,937,000, for a total of $30,870,000: The amounts paid to individuals in the province of Saskatchewan were: Family allowances, $19,450,000; pensions to persons over 70, $19,200,000, or a total of $38,650,000, or a grand total of $69,520,000. Let us get this clear. I am not arguing for a minute that, because these amounts were paid, that in itself is a reason why money should not be paid towards primary education, if it can be shown that after all of these federal payments, and after all of the moneys which that province is able to collect in taxes as a result of the prosperity towards which we have at least in part contributed by the policies of this government, they are in serious need of money, and therefore because of that need cannot support their schools. But, Mr. Speaker, this is the central point upon which my hon. friend's case falls down, namely that under the existing financial arrangements between the dominion and the provinces the provinces do not have enough money to spend upon primary education, if they choose to spend it there, rather than upon roads, bridges and other provincial purposes, which is their right. I sympathize with him; he has done a wonderful job with the material which he had, but he just does not have the facts to support it.
Under this tax agreement the Saskatchewan government has had surpluses every year from April 30, 1944, to March 31, 1951.

What about the federal
government?

On a question of privilege, I have put up no poor mouth for Saskatchewan. I was speaking on behalf of the children of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps that was a harsh way of putting the words of my hon. friend, but I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members, if what my hon. friend did was not this. He said on behalf of the children of Canada: "I would like to see them have a good education; I want more money spent on education, but I want the federal government to spend it." Well, the responsibility for providing the education is that of the provinces, and the only excuse that the provinces have for not -providing it is that they have not the money with which to do it. While perhaps the term that I used was hardly fair, yet essentially my hon. friend's case is that we are asking the federal government to put up this money

because the provinces either have not the money or -they will not spend it in adequate amounts.

May I ask the
minister a question? He said that the federal government -cancelled indebtedness to the extent of $36J million for Saskatchewan. Why was no calculation made for Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To be fair to all concerned, I think one should say that the $36| million represents amounts that were advanced by the federal government to the province of Saskatchewan during the 1930's when the price of the primary product that is turned out there had fallen to its lowest level in four hundred years, and when there was a succession of five or maybe six droughts. Those large amounts of money were advanced to the province for seed grain and relief upon the understanding that the seed grain would be repaid, and when, under conditions which reflect no discredit either upon the provincial government there or upon the people of Saskatchewan in any way, the amounts were not repaid, it was considered proper and fair to everyone concerned that the $36J million should be cancelled. I presume the reason that was not done in Nova Scotia was that the same indebtedness had never been incurred.
I was saying that in the issue of Time of January 19,	1953, the following article
appeared:
Saskatchewan More cornucopias
For 364 days a year, Clarence Melvin Fines dresses like the conservative citizen that he is. But once a year, on the day he delivers his budget to the Saskatchewan legislature, provincial treasurer Fines puts on his gaudiest necktie. What kind of cornucopia does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) put on?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He is also doing a very good job under those excellent policies. The article goes on:
Fines convinced his socialist colleagues that a high credit rating should be the province's goal. "We were under suspicion" he says. "Our financial methods had to be more than orthodox. They had to be ultra-orthodox".
And now as a result of the ultra-orthodox methods applied, I presume in relation to the

cost of primary education and creating a condition upon the strength of it, the hon. member for Saskatoon is urging that more money should be paid by .the federal government. We have this request being made. Well, it reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of one time when I was in the position that Mr. Fines is in now and perhaps the hon. member for Saskatoon was in the position he is in now, and I was applying to Mr. Dunning at that time for more money. He said: "Garson, I am delighted that you should have it as long as you do not take it out of me." In the present case, if the-
And the taxpayers think that, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, perhaps. I think my hon. friend is entirely right because the danger with which we are really faced in connection with this matter of federal subsidies is this. Perhaps the hon. member for Peel made the remark in part facetiously, but it is a very pointed remark just the same. The danger we are faced with is this. We have here an arrangement entered into after long negotiations and great travail, under which provincial treasuries upon the whole have flourished very greatly indeed. And if there is a tendency not to use in their budgets the prosperity which these agreements have brought them in order to discharge carefully their own proper constitutional responsibilities, and if there is a tendency to keep on loading more and more upon the federal government, then the federal taxpayers of this country, like the goose that lays the golden egg, are going to balk.
They have to pay for the schools at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, they have to pay for the schools at home. In other words, it can hardly be maintained that this attitude is reasonable when, during the currency of these tax agreements, the provinces, after increasing their expenditures not only upon education but also upon roads and everything else-very nearly tripling their expenditures over the period of the tax agreements-have an over-all accumulated surplus in the five-year period of nearly two-thirds of a billion dollars.
And yet my hon. friend makes that the basis for his case-that we should provide federal grants to education, to help out provinces which are in that position. Now, I say to my hon. friend that if that is the sort of demand that he is going to make, in the circumstances in which we are at the present time, then he wants to be very, very careful that the point is not reached where the federal 68108-85

taxpayer is going to balk at this and say, "We do not want the agreements at all." And if that were the case, where would his province be?

May I ask
the minister a question? Can the minister inform the house if at any of the dominion-provincial conferences provincial governments have requested from the dominion direct grants for education and, if so, how many of them?
Yes.
The hon. member for Souris says, "Yes". If so, how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I hesitate to speak offhand, from memory, on this matter. But I did make a statement last year, at which time I had somewhat more leisure than I have had on this occasion to check that very point. This is what I said at that time-and if the situation has not changed in the last year, it is still true:
It is commonplace to say that the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures over education is, of all provincial rights, the one of which some if not all of the provinces are most jealous. Therefore, as between federal and provincial governments, the initiative in connection with matters pertaining to education is one which I think the federal government has always felt should be taken by the provincial governments. So far as I am aware, the provincial governments have never raised with the federal government at any time the subject matter of this resolution as such;
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Please let me finish. I am in the embarrassing position of quoting myself because, as I say, I had more leisure last time to prepare. I have not had time to check between last year and now as to whether representations have been made, or have come in, and I do not like to make a definite statement until I make an inquiry. However, I am quoting now what I said at that time-and I think it is still true:
So far as I am aware, the provincial governments have never raised with the federal government at any time the subject matter of this resolution as such; nor have they raised the question of educational costs except as an item of the provincial budgets which naturally were the subject of discussion in the Rowell-Sirois report, in the conference dealing with the dominion proposals of 1945, and indeed in all the fiscal conferences between the federal government and the provinces.
When I say "as such" I mean this, that the provinces have never been willing to concede that the federal government by any means, directly or indirectly, should have any control over their primary educational system. But what they have said is this: "We are addressing ourselves in this conference as to our

Education
educational needs to cover our whole budget. Here it is. We have to provide tor education and we have to provide for health. There it is." It is only in that sense that they have referred to education.
The whole consideration of the Rowell-Sirois commission report was with a view to reaching an agreement under which provincial budgets as a whole could be taken care of. And I am sure that every member will agree that they should have the right to decide, in respect of a matter which comes under their jurisdiction, as to whether they will spend their money upon primary education, or upon highways, or upon roads, or some other way. Surely that is a matter of ordinary common sense.
Surely, from the standpoint of just ordinary, proper administration, where you have three levels of authority, the school administration, the municipal and the provincial, with all their overhead, their rent, their stationery, and all that sort of thing, it is not a fair or prudent expenditure of the taxpayers' money that you should add a fourth level of government, and waste it in that way.
Surely it is a much more sensible arrangement, as the Rowell-Sirois commission recommended, that the provinces should be put in a position where they can arrange their own proper responsibilities, and then leave them there to mind their own business, and not attempt to interfere with them or to supervise them in any way.
Now, my hon. friend will say, "I do not want to supervise them". But does he think for one moment that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) can write out a cheque for, let us say, $50 million or $75 million-and at $5 a head in Canada, if it were at that rate, it would be $75 million-does he think that the Minister of Finance can just write out the cheque and say, "Here you go; you do not have to run your primary education. You do not have to take the responsibility for the expenditure of the money. Just go ahead and spend the money, and we will not take any further notice of the matter, at all."
He cannot do that. If he did, he would have to see that the money which was earmarked for primary education was spent for primary education. And I say again that in any of these schemes people who are said to know something about this matter have been opposed to earmarked grants. And one of the reasons is that it is only when you give a general grant that is not earmarked, a grant to be spent by the province as it, in its own judgment and within its own jurisdiction, chooses to spend it, that you are protecting provincial autonomy.

it would not be willing to accept from the federal government a grant earmarked for education, to be spent on education?
