speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion, as I have in other sessions when such a motion has been before the house, I want to point out that there may be a difference of opinion as to the way in which words are to be interpreted when we are asked to support a motion that consideration should be given to the advisability of expanding and equalizing educational opportunities across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose. It does not seem to me that it is necessary to define in the most minute detail the manner in which the provinces are to be placed in a better position with respect to the financing of education. I take this motion as an attempt to obtain an expression of opinion from the members of the house that in the opinion of this house it is desirable to seek a way in which the provincial governments and the municipalities under them will find it possible to meet the increasing demands of education which are their responsibility.
While the motion does not specifically deal with the municipalities, I recognize that no hon. member can discuss this subject without a full understanding of the place of the municipalities in dealing with this problem.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) did not touch on it.

As has been pointed out, that is where the pinch comes today. Unfortunately the whole speech of the Minister of Justice on this subject completely failed to deal with the position of the municipalities. That is where the problem really rests at this time. As I am sure every hon. member knows, there have been repeated requests from the representatives of the municipalities that in some way their plight with respect to mounting educational costs should be recognized and dealt with.
I propose to deal with the subject not so much from the point of view of the manner in which money might be made available but rather from the point of view of the need of some action to deal with the subject, particularly by the combined consideration of the dominion and provincial governments to find some way in which municipalities across Canada may be able to relieve the burden which is now imposed upon the municipal taxpayer and particularly upon home owners in those municipalities.
It is only necessary to mention the fact without enlarging upon it. The very foundation of our society, the society we seek to strengthen and build by education itself, rests upon the home.
In so far as governments at every level can by their action improve the position of the home owner, they should seek to encourage the owning and improvement of homes, pride in homes and the happiness that may be found in those homes because it is there that the real strength of our society will be found I was impressed by the fact that the Minister of Justice on a number of occasions spoke of the willingness or unwillingness of the federal taxpayer to meet this responsibility if any heavier burden were placed upon the federal taxpayer. Who is the federal taxpayer, Mr. Speaker? There is no such thing as a separate human entity. The federal taxpayer is the provincial taxpayer and the municipal ^ taxpayer. They are the same
+TSS' ln every immunity across anada those who pay taxes pay to the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion government.

I do not feel it is necessary for me to suggest that the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) in presenting this motion contemplates the position of the municipalities. Everyone who has had any practical responsibility for education knows that it is at the municipal level that the basic responsibility rests.

That is where the pinch comes.
68108-85J
So far as they are concerned it is only a question of whether the taxes are taken by one body or another, and most taxpayers from their own experience would prefer to see the larger amount being handled closer to home. They have found that the closer the collection and supervision is to their own point of payment the greater economy there is and the less extravagance of the nature we have seen so plainly exposed in the house during the past couple of weeks. After all it is not only the spending of money that is';

Education
important, it is how the money is spent. What we should be seeking is to get the money paid in a way that will produce the greatest economy and efficiency and the results that are most desirable for the Canadian taxpayer, federal, provincial, or municipal, but the Canadian taxpayer right across Canada who regards education and health as the two most important problems for governments at every level.	.
When the Minister of Justice speaks about the surpluses that have mounted year by year, he ignores the fact that this is very largely the result of the inflation which has been promoted in this country by the methods employed by the dominion government. That inflation has had a great deal to do with the mounting levels of receipts in dollars by the name of dollars. In real money the story is somewhat different, but the story is not different from the point of view of the necessity for increased facilities for education in each community.
I do not intend to engage in a debate as to the general financial methods of the dominion government, although the Minister of Justice has sought to place that before us as an issue at this time. Nor do I propose to extend the discussion that has taken place already so far as the Minister of Justice is concerned, about the comparative advantages of the dominion government's methods and those of the government of Saskatchewan or of any other province. I prefer to deal with this from the point of view of the importance of education, the needs of those who must accept this responsibility, and my own hope that members of this house will see fit to indicate their belief that there is an urgent need- and I repeat "urgent need"-for consideration of this subject which is certainly imposing very serious problems upon every municipal government and every school board in this country at this time.
I am glad that this debate has been brought on now, because it comes forward at a time when it is possible for us to express opinions in anticipation of education week which runs from March 1 to March 7 inclusive. That national effort to impress upon the people of Canada the fact that education is everybody's business does deserve our commendation and support. I believe it will be helpful to those behind that effort to know the attitude of the legislators in this house now in regard to this subject. Also it will be helpful to them to know the view of the provincial legislators and the municipal councils in regard to this subject.
The basic theme of education week, which will be recognized right across Canada in
about five weeks, is to impress upon all Canadians that education is everybody's business-not the business of the dominion government, the provincial government or the municipal government; not the business of the federal taxpayer, the provincial taxpayer, or the municipal taxpayer; but rather the business of every Canadian. And, as Canadians, we should co-operate in every way we can to advance the cause of education right across this country of ours.
No one recognizes better than I do, from personal experience and personal responsibility, the need for drawing a clear distinction between such measure of co-operation as may be extended by the dominion government and the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments and the provincial departments of education for the over-all policy of education within the provinces; and of the school boards and the municipal governments under the provincial governments for education at the local level. I may be forgiven for reminding hon. members that I had for some years direct responsibility as minister of education in one of our provinces.
You did a good job, too.

I had personal contact with the needs of the municipalities and the points of view they expressed. Without in any way raising this as an issue at this time, I need only remind hon. members that I demonstrated my own belief that the municipal taxpayer must be relieved of the burden for education in a very substantial measure.
It was while I was minister of education in one of our provinces that a very substantial part of the cost of education at the municipal level was assumed by that provincial government. I still hold the same opinion. I believe that one of the most important responsibilities of the combined levels of government at this time is to find a way in which the heavily burdened municipal taxpayer will be relieved of the crippling burden of taxation for education and health at the municipal level, which at this time must be placed so largely upon homes and real property.
Hear, hear.

I believe this has two purposes, first of all to give flexibility in revenue, which cannot be possible when the position of the home owner is considered. He may not be a home owner but may be one who rents a home, because both are taxpayers. It should also be considered from the point of view of encouragement of a greater number of people to buy and own their own homes. I think it can be properly and safely said that the greatest protection of our concept of a free society is to have the largest possible number

of Canadians owning their own homes and having them as the centre of their whole social system. I might add that it is a way in which they have a stake in their community, which gives them an added interest in the efficiency and economy that will be practised by their local municipal government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this subject is assuming rapidly increasing importance. Right across Canada statements are being made by responsible citizens that there is immediately ahead of us the threat of a great shortage of qualified teachers for our schools. If that is so-and I find it difficult to doubt that it is so in view of the sources from which those statements come-then it is time for each one of us as a Canadian citizen, even if we completely divorce that position from our responsibility in this parliament, to take a very great and immediate interest in this subject.
The most important factor in education is the teacher. The most important factor in the development of the character of our youth, after the fundamental education which they receive at their mothers' knees and in the churches, is to be found in the standard of education given by teachers across Canada. I think every hon. member of this house will agree that there is a debt of gratitude owed by all Canadians to the unselfish service given to the cause of education by teachers who very often have not been recognized as they should be by the salaries they have received.
It is not merely the academic qualification of the teacher which is important in implanting in the minds of our youth the right approach to the life ahead of them, it is also the spirit and the character of the teacher. The character of our teachers has fully justified the confidence that has been placed in them. It would be impossible, however, for the spirit, the buoyancy and the confidence in our system not to be shaped in some measure by the extent to which those teachers feel that their great responsibility is appreciated by those who fix the level of their salaries.
I have said before in the discussion of this subject, and I do not apologize for repeating it now, that next to those who guide our religious faith there is no calling to which a Canadian can devote himself which plays a more vital part in the life, the character and future of our people, than does the teaching profession. It is many, many centuries ago since it was said by a very wise Greek that the foundation of every state is the education of its youth. Never was that more dramatically true than it is today. The kind of country that Canada is to be ten years, twenty-five years, one hundred years
Education
from now, is going to be determined in a very substantial measure by the kind of education we give our children in our schools.
May I emphasize one vitally important fact recognized by every educator and by everyone who understands the place of education, whether it be in the home, the church or the school. It is in the earliest years of receptive thought that some of the most important guiding principles of life will be established in the minds of our children. Very often in the distant years ahead it will be the principles implanted today in the mind of some young child which will determine whether or not that child will resist temptation, or will accept the responsibilities falling upon him in some great task, or will avoid the pitfalls that are bound to be before everyone. In giving education, we are not merely providing a means by which our children will earn a living and gain some measure of material happiness. We are shaping their whole future; we are shaping the way in which they will meet all the trials that every human being in this and other countries must face today, and will continue to face in the years ahead.
We are not just speaking of academic attainment as a result of education. We are speaking of the character of our people. When we talk of many other things, and seek legislative measures to deal with problems connected with them, we sometimes ignore the fact that most of these problems could be best dealt with by the fundamental education we give our youth. We will have before us shortly the new draft of the Criminal Code containing provisions in regard to offences by young offenders. We are in the habit of speaking of that problem as juvenile delinquency. The most effective way to tackle juvenile delinquency is to be sure that all children, wherever they live and whatever the circumstances of their parents may be, will receive the kind of education that will give them the ethical standards to resist the temptations that are bound to be in their path.
We shall be dealing also with a section of the Criminal Code concerning drunken driving. Far more effective than any law in determining the way in which our people will live, and the manner in which they will face problems of society in this and other respects, is the sense of obligation they will have developed in their own minds to their fellow citizens. The men and women who have been taught as children to remember their obligation to others will be much less likely to get behind the wheel of a car, with all its dreadful possibilities, in a condition that does not meet the responsibility imposed

Education
upon them by that simple act. The same thing is true of all the problems we meet in our daily life, and in respect of which we are called upon to deal from time to time by legislative action. All this I repeat because of the necessity of placing in the hands of municipal authorities and the school boards adequate revenues to bring into the teaching profession the very finest brains and the very best spirit to be found amongst the young people of Canada.
Then may I deal with another subject which is related to this; that is the excellent work being done by home and school organizations right across Canada. At this time over 200,000 Canadians are actively engaged, through this and related organizations, in advancing the cause of education in every province of Canada. There are also the parent-teacher organizations where, from the special knowledge gained by teachers in their own field, they are able to encourage a better understanding of this great problem. I point out also to the minister the importance of adult education in relation to this whole subject of education, because adult education is largely made possible by the broad standards of education developed at the primary level.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question arises as to how we are to encourage into the ranks of the teaching profession the very best of our young university and high school graduates. The question arises also as to how we are to provide the very best educational facilities possible in this country of such tremendous opportunity. This afternoon the discussion has dealt in some measure with the difficulty of drawing the distinction between the provincial responsibility and the responsibility of the dominion government. I am not suggesting for one moment that anything should be done which will in any way, indirectly or directly, encourage the dominion government to invade the field of education. I agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and others who have spoken on this subject on earlier occasions, as I have asserted at dominion-provincial conferences. I have attended, that there is no subject of provincial jurisdiction in regard to which the provincial governments will more jealously assert their prerogative. I hope they will continue to do so. Our unity as a nation depends upon the extent to which we recognize the position of the provincial government in the field of education and do not, directly or indirectly at any level, seek to interfere with that responsibility.
Education, for reasons so obvious they need not be repeated here, was left to the provincial governments at the time the provinces
fMr. Drew.]
of Canada joined to form one nation in 1867. When the Minister of Justice today warned us that we must be cautious in this respect and that it would be unwise to undertake a system of grants in aid which would force the dominion government to exercise some measure of control over the expenditure, I wonder whether that same observation applies with equal force to every other place where the dominion government is now making grants of one kind and another. That is exactly the point I have been seeking to make in this house on a number of occasions with regard to other grants. I believe that the best way for us to assure the continuing strength of our federal system is to make sure that the provincial governments and the municipal councils within those provinces have adequate revenues so they are able to carry out their tasks without any possibility of intervention at any time by the dominion government.
That was the concept of confederation that we accepted in 1867. It is the genius of our form of confederation. It is the basis upon which national unity has been established here. When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) told us that at present there are agreements which have been found satisfactory to the provinces-and may I say that I realize why he is not now present; he indicated that it was necessary for him to keep some appointment-and that Ontario, which recently signed the agreement, finds it satisfactory, I would remind him of something which I hope he has not forgotten, namely that most of the provinces have stated-and certainly the government of the province of Ontario has done so in the most emphatic terms-that these agreements are not a satisfactory solution of the problem. In signing this agreement strictly as a temporary measure the premier of Ontario said that at best it was only a stopgap, and that steps should be taken immediately to find a system by which the provincial governments and the municipalities would have adequate sources of revenue.
Not long ago I saw the report of a speech by the premier of Nova Scotia to the bar association of that province in which he said that the time had come when the people in this country must decide whether there is going to continue to be a federal system in Canada. He left no doubt about his own belief that if we follow the present course of stripping the provinces of their real provincial authority, the federal system in Canada cannot continue. Similar statements in different words have been made by the heads of other provincial governments. My own belief is

that the one way in which to deal satisfactorily with this subject is to seek a reallocation of the taxes which are given to the provincial governments and to the municipalities under them, with independence of revenue which is consistent with their independent responsibilities in their own field, and that this be done without further delay.
It is all very well to point out that the provincial governments are receiving large sums of money from the dominion government under agreements whereby the provinces gave up, for the time being, their historic tax fields; I refer to the great basic fields of the personal income tax, the corporation tax and other taxes which have been the subject of agreement. What the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) refrained from dealing with was the fact that, having obtained agreements in this respect, the dominion government continues to invade still further the general field of taxation, so that the percentage of the tax dollar available to both the municipal and the provincial governments becomes smaller and smaller.
In 1951 the dominion government collected 77 per cent of every dollar paid in taxes by Canadian taxpayers. Last year it would appear that they collected 78 per cent. The figure is going up all the time. Year by year the percentage of the tax dollar available to the provincial and municipal governments becomes less and less. This fact has the effect of forcing back upon the home owner, the tenant and the small businessman in the municipality a larger and larger burden for education and health within the municipality. One of the most urgent needs of the Canadian taxpayer at this time is for governments at all levels to bring about a readjustment of taxation which will relieve the burden of the municipal taxpayer.
I support this motion not with the thought that there may be complete agreement as to the way in which this objective will be worked out. I thought the hon. member for Saskatoon was extremely fair in the way in which he placed before us his own belief that it was not necessary to define in too great detail the procedure by which this proposal is to be put into effect, but rather that we should seek from the members of this house an expression of opinion that at every level of government there be that appropriate consideration of this subject which will make it possible to provide the educational standards that we would wish to see in every part of Canada. He spoke about Canadian children in every part of this country. I believe that is the way in which we should approach the matter. I have indicated my own belief that nothing which is done here at any time must minimize in the slightest measure
Education
the full responsibility of the provincial governments for the vitally important subject of education and, under them, the municipal authorities who operate under provincial laws and who deal at the local level with this tremendously important subject in the building of a strong and good society.
Without seeking to draw differences between one party and another as to any political doctrine they may express from time to time with respect to financial or other matters, but having regard to the vital importance of education at this time, to the place of the teacher in the building of this nation, to the schools and the physical requirements of education itself I would therefore hope that all of us will say in no uncertain terms that, with a full recognition of the constitutional responsibilities of the provinces and the municipalities, we want the dominion government which now absorbs so much of every tax dollar to do what they can to bring the governments together to see whether there is not some way in which we can broaden the basis of education for the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we have had the opportunity of debating this resolution on three previous occasions. Much credit is due the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) for the persistence which he has displayed in pressing toward a very important objective. In approaching the resolution, I should like to think in terms of an objective. The resolution is quite clear as far as I am concerned. It merely asks the government to take into consideration the advisability of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
The hon. member for Saskatoon indicated clearly that across Canada from coast to coast support for the objective or the proposition is growing, and it is not support emanating merely from any one political party. It is a feeling which members of school boards are supporting. The ratepayers themselves generally are supporting it. Certainly the teachers are supporting it, as are all others who have given careful and serious consideration to the present problem which confronts us in connection with financing education.
I was rather amazed at some of the arguments advanced today by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in an effort, I presume, to indicate to the Liberal membership in the house that they should not support the resolution at this time even though possibly the vast majority of them do in their own minds

Education
agree with it. As a matter of fact I was somewhat interested when the hon. member for Saskatoon indicated that certain persons who did not belong to his political party suggested that it might be wise to climb on the bandwagon at this time because this thing is going to happen sooner or later.
The Minister of Justice devoted considerable time last year to another resolution couched in the same language. At that time he made it perfectly clear that as far as certain truisms, as he called them, were concerned, all hon. members are in agreement. At page 616 of Hansard of March 20, 1952, he said:
From what has been said it is clear that certain points of agreement have emerged. It is hardly necessary for example to repeat all the truisms about the great importance of education in our national life.
Well, I would concede, Mr. Speaker, that there would be no disagreement among us in this house as far as that matter is concerned. He goes on to say:
Nor is it necessary to argue at great length that teachers' salaries in general are inadequate; for their inadequacy is clearly established by the relative economic unattractiveness of the teaching profession.
In the light of the information which was placed on Hansard on March 19 of last year by the hon. member for Saskatoon, I would doubt very much whether any hon. member would disagree with that assertion. I wonder how many hon. members gave consideration to the table which the house granted the hon. member permission to have included in Hansard. May I refer to one column, Mr. Speaker, headed "Median salaries of teachers in all schools, 1950." I know the general situation has improved somewhat since that time, as far as certain teachers are concerned, but there has not been any substantial improvement. In one province the median salary of teachers is $1,083; in another $1,341; in another $2,109; in still another $1,689; in another $1,580; in another $2,279, and the highest is $2,668. The last one I give is $966, which is the lowest. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is not another professional group in Canada whose median salaries are anywhere near as low as those. There is no group in the country of organized labourers whose salaries are not substantially higher than those listed here; yet, Mr. Speaker, there is not a group of people in the country who are performing a more necessary or more important service for the country.
When speaking last year the Minister of Justice said at page 617 of Hansard:
It may be stated that the general agreement in this house upon most of the principles which have been enunciated so far in this debate affords a

much more satisfactory basis for examination of the facts than would be the case if we were in disagreement on those principles.
Well, that is fine. According to my way of thinking that is a statement of fact, but it is so significant that last year the Minister of Justice centred practically his entire argument upon what he called "a vital attack upon provincial autonomy." That seemed to be the keynote of the speech which he delivered on March 20 last. Well, it was a specious argument, Mr. Speaker, because there was no vital attack upon provincial autonomy at all, and it was asserted time and time again that there was no intention to interfere with provincial responsibility in the field of the administration of education.
I may also point out that last year the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) carried forward into his speech the keynote which was established by the Minister of Justice. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said in 1951, in referring to the constitutional position: "The provinces have been given exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education. National unity is predicated upon it."
I recall that in closing his speech the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that "we believe that the best way of giving every child in this country the best possible opportunity for education in accordance with her or his talent... is to do it within the terms of the constitution. We believe it is better to do it in that way than by following a suggestion which cannot be accepted"-he was very specific in that-"because it is a matter wholly within the competence of another legislative authority and alien to our own."
It was pointed out to the government last year, and it was also pointed out to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that under section 92, subsection 7, of the British North America Act the establishment, maintenance and management of all hospitals, outside of marine hospitals, falls exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Look at what has happened in that particular field, Mr. Speaker. The federal government is making grants to the provinces. It is true they are earned grants; in other words, they are matched dollar for dollar, and there has to be general agreement as to the nature of the edifice that is to be constructed. Those grants are performing a very valuable service. They are appreciated, and they enable the provinces to provide a much higher standard of hospitalization and general health service for the people. But the point is that we cannot forget that under the British North America Act the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Liberal government

could not have given one dollar in grants to the provinces to assist in hospital construction had they followed the argument used by the Minister of National Health and Welfare last year and the argument used by the Minister of Justice last year and referred to again today.
It is an established fact, the constitution to the contrary notwithstanding, that the provinces and the federal government have been able to get together, even where these fields of exclusive jurisdiction existed, to permit the federal government to make grants to the province to enable them to do certain desirable things. And it could be done just as effectively and as easily in this field as in the field of national health and welfare.
I was particularly interested in hearing what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said today about a grant that is being made for the construction of a school in Winnipeg. The minister appeared to be thrown back on his heels when that was brought to his attention. His "out" was: Well, after all, a certain amount of federal authority is bound to be exercised in connection with the construction of that school.
If the provinces and the federal authorities agree that that shall be the case so far as capital construction is concerned, then certainly the principle could very easily be carried into this general field of education. And may I assert that through grants for capital construction-call them earned grants if you will-the federal government could perform a most valuable function and be of inestimable assistance in this whole field of education by giving consideration to that very aspect of the matter.
This resolution does not tie the government down to any specific course of action. It does not bind the government to make grants for elementary education to provincial departments of education, in turn perhaps to be matched and turned over to local authorities. It does not fie the government down to that at all. Its objective could be reached, in part, through assistance in capital construction, as is the case with respect to hospitals, and with the same end result. This could be done without interference in the administration of schools, any more than today there is interference in the administration of hospitals because earned grants have been made for the construction of or for additions to hospitals.
Since the resolution does not tie the federal government down, I shall offer a suggestion we have offered on previous occasions, namely that it should remove the sales tax from vehicles used in conveying children to 68108-86
Education
schools. In other words it should remove that tax from school buses. Those buses would have to be used exclusively for the purpose intended. There, however, is an example of how the federal authorities could enable the provinces to move toward that objective.
Then of course we have the question of the sales tax and import duties on many of the publications used in the schools. Surely that would be one method of contributing toward the attainment of this objective. But today the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) developed another tack when he said that any move toward making grants to the provinces to effect the objective set forth in the resolution might create a serious unbalance so far as federal-provincial financial relationships are concerned.
Throughout the entire speech by the minister one would almost be obliged to assume, if he did not know otherwise, that the existing agreements between the federal government and the provinces are satisfactory, that they meet the requirements of the provinces, and that they are fair. I deny that suggestion most vehemently. All hon. members know that during the war the provinces willingly moved out of certain tax fields in an effort to achieve victory in military conflict. They were assured that this was but a temporary arrangement. Yet when the war was over they were pressured into a continuation of those agreements. And because the federal government can go into the entire tax field it has been able to pull a squeeze play on the provinces and, in cases, compel them to enter into agreements, even though the terms of those agreements were not satisfactory.
I was interested in a discussion which took place while the Minister of Justice was speaking. He referred to a cancellation of debt in Saskatchewan to the extent of $38,500,000. Of course my mind went back to the fact that we, in my province of Alberta, had also accumulated a huge debt as a consequence of drought and depression. The farmers of my province had accumulated terrific debts; but there was no federal cancellation of them. Perhaps this was because there had been a change of government in that province. The burden was left upon the provincial government in Alberta to cancel debt to the extent of $22 million. I well recall that in the report of the Bank of Canada for 1937 it was stated that the position in my province had improved so materially that the bank would not have been justified in recommending such cancellation. That was political hogwash; we know the reason for it. However, I mention that only in passing.

Education
Under the division of constitutional authority and responsibility as it existed at the time of confederation, things may have been reasonably fair. But as the years have gone by greater and greater responsibilities have been placed upon the shoulders of provincial and municipal governments. It is my conviction that where responsibility exists there should also exist the authority to carry out that responsibility.
The minister spoke in terms of high budgets in the provinces. That is true; but I know of no province in western Canada wherein the percentage increases in grants for education have not exceeded by far the percentage increases in provincial revenue.
Even though it annoys some people, I think I may be forgiven for referring to the province from which I come. It is as natural for me to do so as it was the other evening for the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald), when he referred to Alberta instead of Manitoba. After all, he comes from Alberta, and is presumed to be more familiar with it. I know that in my own province in the fiscal year 1935-36 the gross grant for education was approximately $1,450,000, whereas in the fiscal year 1952-53 it was approximately $9,850,000, or an increase of approximately seven and one-half times the figure for the first year. Yet in that period of time provincial revenues had increased by approximately only four and one-half times the former amount.

It has been so from the very beginning of the province and that system has produced marvellous results if we compare the present situation with what it was in the early days.
In our province, education comes under the department of the provincial secretary, which has authority over the Public Education Council-Conseil de lTnstruction publique-made up of the superintendent, of one member of the government, of catholic bishops and of protestant clergymen. All that to show that in the province of Quebec the rights of everyone, whatever be his nationality or religion, are protected. By the way, I must say that protestant and English-speaking minorities of the province of Quebec are treated as fairly as the majority.
Am I saying these things to draw a comparison with what may have happened in the past in certain provinces with respect to my French-Canadian compatriots? Such a conclusion may be drawn from my remarks. However, I have always thought that generosity played a great part in the conduct of the affairs of the world, and if we, from the province of Quebec, have been generous towards certain elements, it is to be hoped that the same generosity may be displayed by other provinces, where sometimes our feelings have been hurt.

At the beginning, salaries were extremely low; however, the standard of education has always been high. Why? Because we have always believed that when teachers fulfil their task through sheer devotion to duty, more skill is displayed and better results are obtained than when one's salary is the only incentive.
In 1760, after the conquest, though only
60,000	French Canadians remained in the country, education was essential for this nucleus of heroes wanted to remain alive as a racial group.
Have they succeeded? I answer yes. If teaching continued in Quebec in those days, it was thanks to women of gentle birth who had remained in this country and thanks, also, to our parish priests. I spoke of people of gentle birth. It has been claimed that none remained in the province of Quebec after the conquest, but the truth is that many had remained. In every family now, there is still some noble blood. In any event these gentlewomen taught without remuneration, as well as the priests who gave children lessons in arithmetic, grammar and catechism, not to speak of loyalty. Here is an example of this.
In 1866, during the Fenian raids, when the Americans had decided to capture Canada, had the French-Canadian clergy not enjoined the faithful to remain loyal to the British crown, Canada would no more be a jewel in this crown, but we would have been absorbed by the United States of America.

The people in Toronto said of our premier of the time that he knew what he was talking about, that he was an authority.
It was then that this famous Bonne Entente movement came into being and it has never ceased to gain ground. I do wish to pay this tribute to the Catholic clergy, without whom, as I say, we would have been absorbed by our great neighbour to the south.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution that is before us, which has been moved by my deskmate the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), is extremely simple. One is really surprised! that such a simple resolution should call forth such great opposition from the government benches. All this resolution asks is that we in this house express an opinion as to whether or not the government should take into consideration the granting of financial assistance to the provinces for the purpose of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity. The resolution simply asks the house to express its opinion as to whether or not it is advisable for the government to consider the making of such financial grants to the provinces for the purpose specified.
That resolution is based: on the premise that every Canadian child has a birthright. That birthright is an educational opportunity equal to that of any other child in this country. That birthright is an equal educational opportunity whether that child be English or French; whether it be protestant, catholic, jew or gentile; and regardless of race, colour, the economic status of its parents or the part of Canada in which it is born. That is the premise upon which we ask this house?

Education
to consider whether or not this government should grant financial assistance to the provinces in order to enable them to give Canadian children what is their birthright.
The resolution is also based on the premise that today there exists a crisis in education. I do not need to emphasize the importance of education in the building of Canadian citizenship. Its importance, I take it for granted, is accepted by every member of this house. What we are faced with is a crisis. A conservative estimate prepared for Canadian education week shows that in 1955, two years hence, there will be a shortage of
25.000	teachers in Canada. The shortage of teachers in Canada has been increasing every year. By 1955 there will be need for another
1.000	schools to be built. Some municipalities are already finding it extremely difficult to build those schools. Classrooms are already overcrowded and the overcrowding is getting worse.
As has been pointed out by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) and others, some steps must be taken to meet this crisis. If we are to continue to provide educational opportunity for Canadian children we must take some steps which will enable us to staff the schools with properly qualified teachers and to provide sufficient classrooms to accommodate the pupils who are coming to our schools. There has already been pointed out in this house the difference which exists in educational opportunity as between the provinces, in so far as that equality or inequality of opportunity can be measured by the expenditures which have been made for education. In 1950 the median salary of teachers in all schools ranged, as has been pointed out, from $966 in Newfoundland to $2,668 in British Columbia. I think most of us will realize that so long as you have that difference between the salaries which are paid to teachers in different provinces, you are not going to have anything approximating equality of opportunity. You cannot secure in Newfoundland, for less than $1,000 a year, the best and brightest of the young people of that province that we require to enter the teaching profession. If the teaching profession is to attract our best young people, we must be prepared to do something in those provinces that are still paying in the vicinity of $1,000 to $1,500 for teachers.
There has been a persistent decrease in the number of teachers attending our training schools. Last year that decrease was shown in every province in Canada, and ranged from a drop of 10 per cent in Ontario to one of 37 per cent in Prince Edward Island. There was no single province in

Canada that was not affected by that reduction in the number of people attending the teacher training schools.
Those are the facts that we must face. In view of the importance of education, it would seem to me we should be able to face those facts without having regard for political expediency, without having regard for politics, race or religion. It would seem to me that in this house we ought to be able to put the interests of young Canadians first in our discussion of this subject; we should be able to rise above politics, above race, above religion in discussing this question.
In that respect the speech made this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was very disappointing. That speech will be a disappointment to everyone interested in education in this country. It will be a disappointment to the tens of thousands of school teachers across Canada from the provinces in the east to our province on the west coast. That speech will be a disappointment to every school board across this country. It will be a disappointment to a great many national organizations which over the years have been supporting federal aid to education.
The minister's speech this afternoon was based on one premise only, namely political expediency. The minister refused to face up to the crisis that confronts us in our educational systems across this country, and to place in paramount importance the needs of the young people of Canada. He raised a number of objections. It was interesting to find the minister going back to the Rowell-Sirois report and taking therefrom arguments to be used in his stand against this resolution. It is strange indeed how the minister and the government can use this report when it suits their purpose, and completely ignore it and other reports when that suits their purpose. The minister pulled out of the Rowell-Sirois report this afternoon the objections which the authors of that report made to federal aid for education. To my knowledge it is the only time the minister has ever gone to that report for any positive direction on any policy.
I know something about that report. I had the privilege of appearing before that commission, in my capacity as chairman of the Canadian Teachers' Federation, and presenting the opinions of the Canadian teachers. We were disappointed with the point of view expressed in that report; but times have changed since then, and in any case the authors of that report recognized the validity of some of our arguments. They recognized that the demands of education have gone far

Education
beyond those which existed when the British North America Act was adopted. They also pointed out the importance of equal educational opportunities, and at page 51 they said:
It is our hope that provision can be made for the fiscal needs of all provinces, including within those needs provision for the education of the young.
While the Rowell-Sirois report does not recommend specific grants for education, it does express the hope that the federal government will make available to the provinces such financial aid as will enable those provinces to meet the costs of education and provide equal educational opportunity within the provinces. That in reality is all that we ask in this resolution. All we ask is that the government give consideration to granting financial aid to the provinces to enable them in turn to provide equal educational opportunity to our Canadian children.
The minister placed a great deal of importance upon the fact that the federal government could not give grants to the provinces for education without at the same time exercising some control over education within the provinces. The federal government has been providing millions of dollars for education within the provinces in one way or another, and we have yet to hear in any province a single voice raised to the effect that the federal government is, by reason of those grants, interfering with provincial rights in the matter of education. The Minister of Justice was simply raising this argument because this government does not want to provide such federal assistance to the provinces; or is it, with a federal election in the offing, afraid of the political effects of any such grants?
If this government has the interest of young Canadians at heart it will consider ways and means by which it can come to the assistance of the provinces in this matter. The minister asked, where is the federal government going to get the money to pay for federal aid to education? During the war we never hesitated for a moment to find money to educate our soldiers. We had to open what amounted to public schools in some of the army camps in order to teach some of our young men to read and write so they might be able to follow the instructions which were handed out to them. We had to undertake the provision of elementary education in some of these camps. We never hesitated to train young people for work in the munition plants. When war comes we can find money for education or for any other purpose. If this government wanted to find
money and allocate it to assist the provinces in providing better education for the youth of this country, they could do so.
The minister tried to tell us that the provinces are able to provide better educational opportunities if they so desire. He may be in a much better position to judge that than I am. What I do know is that in the province of Ontario the municipal taxpayers are still called upon to bear a very large share of the cost of education. What I do know is that in some of the suburban municipalities of Toronto we have found it difficult to have new houses built because those municipalities were unable to bear the extra cost that would be involved if large numbers of new homes were to be built there. Upon occasions private contractors have been required by the municipalities to include in the cost of the homes the added cost of building schools, with the understanding that this would be added to the selling price of a home, so that a purchaser would absorb not only the cost of the land, the interest on his mortgage and local improvement charges but also the cost of building schools in the municipality.
It may be that provincial governments are in a better financial position than they were. But if they are, they are not coming to the relief of municipal taxpayers to an extent that will relieve those taxpayers of this overburden, and provide equal educational opportunity for all our children.
I pointed out that much is being done now by the federal government, and that it has been done without any interference with provincial rights. But we have had to have recourse to many subterfuges to obtain that assistance. We make large contributions to education through the Department of Labour, and try to kid ourselves into believing that this is not a contribution to education. We are told that because it is made through the Department of Labour, therefore it is a contribution to labour. The Department of Veterans Affairs makes heavy contributions to education. There again we are told this is not an assistance to education but that technically it is to assist our veterans. The Department of National Defence makes contributions to education, but we kid ourselves into believing that these are not educational grants, that they do not interfere with provincial rights, that they simply help our Department of National Defence.
The Department of National Health and Welfare contributes in a number of ways to educational projects. But we camouflage that by placing these expenditures under this department, and thereby convince ourselves that we are avoiding any interference with

provincial rights in the field of education. The national research council, with its scholarships for educational purposes, enters the picture. Here again we are told this is not a direct aid to education. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration is also in the picture. This department finds it is quite constitutional to assist immigrant children and adults by helping to provide schools for them. Yet the department appears to take the view that it would not be constitutional for the government to assist native-born Canadian children through regular educational channels. The Department of Trade and Commerce, particularly through the educational division of the dominion bureau of statistics, makes its contribution. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and other activities connected with the federal government, either directly or indirectly make their contributions to education.
I have here the table referred to by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) which shows that all the provinces, through the Department of Labour, have accepted federal grants for youth training in the last three years in an amount well over a million dollars. Every province in Canada has taken advantage of this. I find, for instance, that Quebec took the largest share, amounting to $350,000. Ontario accepted $180,000. The truth is that every province accepts federal moneys for youth training. Yet we are asked to believe that, in some way, this differs from federal aid to be given to a regular school system.
While these large sums can be spent for youth training, apparently without any interference with provincial rights, if one suggests the making of grants to secondary or primary academic schools, then there is the suggestion that in some mysterious way there will be some interference with provincial control of education.
We give grants to train persons for gainful employment, and the provinces appear to have no objection to accepting federal moneys for this purpose-provided, of course, that such gainful employment is not such as would be secured from an academic course of studies. We are told that if the expenditure is for academic education then, on constitutional grounds, it must be ruled out. We see that in the last three years nearly $6 million has been paid out of the federal treasury to assist vocational schools, and these sums have been accepted by all the provinces Df Canada. I have not heard it suggested anywhere that the giving of this assistance for vocational education has interfered in any ivay with provincial rights. The suggestion

is made that if the money came through the Department of Labour it could not be classified as educational aid.
Then in the last three years we have provided nearly $4 million in payments to provinces by way of capital expenditure on vocational schools. For the life of me I cannot see the difference between providing money to build vocational schools which train plumbers, automobile mechanics and the like, and making grants to schools that provide training so that one may become a lawyer, a doctor or a school teacher. These are some of the subterfuges we have to accept so that the federal government may make grants for education without, at the same time, appearing to interfere with provincial rights.
Education in Canada has suffered for a long time-as a matter of fact I suppose all through our history-because of the rivalry between race and race, religion and religion. I am told that the people of the province of Quebec do not want to accept federal aid. They fear that in some way the state will interfere with religious training in then-schools. I find that in Ontario a large section of the province is afraid that if federal aid for education is extended, the Roman Catholics in Ontario or Quebec are going to benefit by such assistance. What is happening in the province of Ontario is that in order that the province may take advantage of federal grants for vocational schools at the secondary school level, the standards and requirements have been lowered for entrance to such secondary schools. Thus each year thousands of pupils are entering the secondary schools who can thereby be assisted by the federal grants that are made at the secondary school level -I am referring to vocational schools- whereas if they were kept back in the grades below grade 9 they would not be assisted at all by federal grants.
Is it not time in this country that we should consider the question of educational opportunity on its own merits? Surely it is just as important to a French-speaking Roman Catholic child living in Quebec to have a good education as it is to an English-speaking Protestant child living in Ontario. Surely we are able to forget our political differences in this house on the question of education. Surely we are able to forget our language and religious differences and unite to give to every Canadian child what is his birthright, the best educational opportunity that Canada -not Ontario, not Quebec, not Newfoundland-can provide.

Mr. Speaker, this is a most interesting and important subject,

and I feel that the time is fast approaching when we will have to do something about it besides just talk. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has brought this subject to our attention on a number of occasions, and each time it has been talked out. This afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) presented arguments which I assume he considered were strong enough to persuade the house not to pass the resolution now before us. He pointed out particularly, as we all know, that education is something which, under the British North America Act, belongs to the provinces. I believe he quoted section 93 which says in part:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education-
I am sure we all agree with that. That is as it should be. From reading our history books we know that if such an arrangement had not been made at the time of confederation by the fathers of confederation, it is very doubtful whether we would have the country that is Canada today. I know every hon. member here gives wholehearted support to the principle laid down at that time, and that no hon. member would wish to see it changed. However, I believe we can still support the resolution without feeling that it detracts in the slightest from the spirit or the letter of the British North America Act.
Hon. members who have spoken have pointed out that Canada is one country, and although we have ten different educational systems we all agree that equal opportunity should be given to each and every young Canadian. In the days of confederation education was not such a must as it is today. We remember that in the early days education was more or less looked upon as a sort of luxury for only the rich people, or for some of our professional people. It was felt that the majority of our citizens could very well get along without any advanced or even elementary education. As we progressed, elementary education in our schools took on the concept that there were three subjects which it was necessary for every child to know, reading, writing and arithmetic. I think this still should be the basis of our education in Canada today.
In addition, however, we all know that in the last twenty-five or thirty years we have advanced along technical lines. Today a boy or girl in a chosen walk of life must have a technical education. The farmer today must know far more than he knew a few years ago. The man who works in the forests, the mines or anywhere else must have a far better education today than twenty-five, thirty or forty years ago.

This leads me to mention costs. If we are to have better education it means greater cost to the people, the provinces and the municipalities, and that has been the case. In the early days only a very small portion of our taxes went for education. Today education is the biggest problem with which provinces and municipalities have to deal. It has become such a problem in my own province of New Brunswick and its municipalities that it is practically impossible for the people to bear the burden that has been placed upon them.
Mention was made this afternoon of the training of teachers and the great scarcity of teachers in Canada today. Someone said there is a shortage of 2,500 teachers in our schools. We also have this problem in New Brunswick, and today in many schools we are using locally licensed teachers who are very poorly trained. We also are using married women who, I may say, deserve great credit for having responded to the call and given up their work in their homes to go out and help with our education.

We have no estimate of the cost of the loss of those young people to our part of the country but there is no question in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that it has cost the maritime provinces millions of dollars in the past to educate young men and young women who have gone to Ontario, Quebec and western Canada. As I say, I think for that reason we have a special claim against the rest of Canada in that regard.
I will just quote the resolution, Mr. Speaker:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I contend that the words "expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada" presuppose that education in certain provinces is not as good as it is in others, and that educational opportunities in

Education
certain provinces are not as good as they are in other provinces. There is no doubt in my mind that some of the richer provinces of Canada could and should help themselves. There is no reason why the federal government should give much help to the rich province of Ontario or to the proportionately still richer province of Alberta; but there is every reason in the world why provinces like Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland should receive special attention in this regard.
I would also like to point out in this connection, Mr. Speaker, that I feel we in the east have another strong argument for more assistance in the matter of education. It will be remembered that since confederation the three maritime provinces have not been able to extend their boundaries. In 1867 when the act of confederation, the British North America Act, was passed there were great lands known as the public domain of this country which belonged, as we thought, to every province in Canada. Since confederation the boundaries of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and even British Columbia, have been extended away to the north. We all know the great and almost unlimited wealth that has flowed to those provinces as a result of this extension of their boundaries. I claim that is a second reason why we in the east, circumscribed as we are, who have contributed so much to the progress and development of this country, deserve special consideration in this regard.
I would also like to point out that in my opinion the federal government has a special responsibility and obligation in connection with education. The federal parliament is responsible for the defence of this country. We know that during the last war when they were seeking recruits for the armed farces, many of the young men in Canada were turned down because they did not have sufficient education. If the government of Canada is going to call on its young men to operate tanks, airplanes and any of the other technical equipment used in war today they should also be responsible in the same way for seeing that these young men are qualified from an educational standpoint. There is also the question of federal civil servants, many thousands of whom are recruited from different parts of Canada. The federal government requires quite exacting standards of education of its civil servants and, if all parts of Canada are to be equally represented in the civil service of this country, they must all have equal opportunity of providing themselves with that education.
I spoke a moment ago about the poorer provinces. There is no question in my mind that the time must come, and must come soon, when these provinces which are so heavily taxed at the present time will have to receive further assistance in order to carry on their different services. I might say that my own province of New Brunswick is the most heavily taxed province in Canada today. If you look at the statistics for 1950 you will find that the per capita debt of Quebec was only $92.24. The province of New Brunswick had a per capita debt of $286.62. Anyone can see the great disparity between those provinces in the matter of per capita debt. I could go on and quote figures for the other provinces to show that disparities exist between them.
There is also a comparison of debt charge to revenue in the different provinces. The figure for Alberta, for instance, was 6 * 6 per cent, and that was the lowest in Canada. The New Brunswick figure is 23-8 per cent, one of the highest in Canada. This great discrepancy is one of the reasons it is difficult for some of the provinces to bear the burden which they are trying to bear.
I said a moment ago, and I think I can repeat, that a rich province should not receive aid. The minister this afternoon mentioned something about an item of $5 per head of population, or some amount of that kind. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that money should be distributed in that manner. It should be distributed, if an act is put through this federal house, according to the needs of the different provinces. If one province needed $1 per head, that is the amount that should be paid to it. If some other province needs $5 that is what they should receive.
I might say that while we are having so much difficulty raising money to look after the schools in our province, I do not think our schools have been neglected. I know that in previous debates in this house the maritime provinces have been held up as a horrible example. Well, anyone who is acquainted with the educational history of this country knows that in years past we have made as good provision, if not better, for the education of our young as any other province in Canada. I might say that in recent years in the province of New Brunswick we have built many fine schools. There are no better schools in Canada than you will find in our province. We have also increased the salaries of our teachers, and today I think the minimum salary of a teacher in our province is $1,200 a year. I forget what the average salary is. We have

also improved the equipment in our schools. But in order to keep up the schools in the province it has been necessary to neglect some of our other services. For instance, our roads or some other public services of that kind have had to be neglected.
I do not believe it is necessary for me to labour this point, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has pointed out that there are many precedents for assistance from the federal government to the provincial government. He spoke about the vocational school assistance, as well as the assistance for veterans and the money which is now being paid to the universities of our country as a result of the Massey report. To my mind this is indeed a responsibility which the federal government must assume within a short time. Again I say I do not believe there is any necessity at all for the federal government to interfere with the rights of the provinces in so far as schools are concerned. As a matter of fact the provinces would not stand for such a thing.
If we are to have well educated people in Canada, if we are going to give the boys and girls in Canada the education to which they are entitled, then the provinces must have the money to provide this education. How it is to be done I do not think poses any great problem of statesmanship. Surely in this House of Commons, in the government of this country, the means can be found. I am sure that if it is the will of this house, a way certainly can be found.
