Mr. Speaker, the motion we are now debating surely has one good point, that is to bring the attention of members of the house to the important matter of education.
I understand that the majority of the previous speakers stressed particularly the dangers that may arise from the constitutional point of view. I have no intention of lengthening the debate on that aspect of the matter, although I may say a few words about it towards the end of my remarks.
I would like to digress for a moment and say something about the danger facing education as well as the way in which we seem to shrink away from our responsibilities towards the young people it is our duty to educate.
Education
I have here an item published in the Toronto Star, giving the results of a survey made in the United States regarding for instance the religious guidance given our youth. The man who made the survey found that 20 per cent of our young people are well educated, especially in the United States, while 20 per cent only are recognized as having religious principles.
This survey shows that, far from being radical, the young people seemed little concerned about giving their own opinion; they are especially, to a certain degree, and in the broader sense of the word, conservative with respect to the principles on which they could base their answers to the questions that were asked. According to the report, less than 20 per cent of those who were questioned, that is, 1,935, whose ages range from 18 to 29, answered that they found little guidance in religion in deciding either how to live, or what political principles to adopt, for instance, with regard to relations between races. This survey showed also that there is nothing to prove that those who believe in God will show more tolerance towards other races than those who have no religious principles, that is the agnostics; as a matter of fact, the latter are more inclined to think that all races should be considered equal. That certainly is not the Roman Catholic theory; we hold that the human being is a noble being, that every man is holy, be he white or black.
As far as opinions about sex are concerned it would seem that our young people tend to seek a better understanding of these matters. About one-third of those interviewed believe that there should be no hushing up of theories about sex. According to them this is neither necessary nor desirable.
I am still on the subject of education, Mr. Speaker. Here are some statistics because I do wish the house to understand that we have enormous responsibilities towards our young people, especially as concerns the guidance our teachers must give them. Our teachers must instruct our young people, they must take charge of them when our boys and girls leave home to go to school or college.
With regard to politics-still according to the inquiry-the more the young men get away from religion, the less they consider that the Democratic and Republican principles are adequate to meet the nation's

Education
needs. Of course, if on account of some shortcoming in our educational system, our professors do not attach enough importance to the advice they give to young people in regard to various forms of governments that may exist in the world, for instance in regard to social security, government controls or state paternalism, it is imperative that the competent authorities guide our professors in these particular fields, so that they may acquire a more detailed knowledge of the various kinds of governments and political theories, in order that they may be in a better position to show our young people how to be better able to judge the good or bad influence they may derive from certain political theories.
There are many who believe, for instance, that there is an enormous difference between the philosophy of nazism and the communist philosophy. I shall quote Marx and Hitler to prove that the difference exists rather as to details, but not as to principles.
According to Marx, the democratic concept of man is false because it is Christian. Democracy claims that each man is a sovereign being. That is the dream and illusion of Christianity.
As for Hitler, he says: to the Christian doctrine claiming that each man has an immortal soul, I oppose with perfect clarity the redeeming doctrine of the nullity and insignificance of the human being.
I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, that our education must absolutely be directed in such a way that our young men and women may have a more detailed knowledge of the different economic and philosophic systems, in order that they may profit from the benefits that our democratic institutions may provide them. It results therefrom that, in addition to the social science studies contained in our programs, some particular stress should be put on the study of social security, not only from a material point of view, but also from the intellectual, spiritual and moral angles. Indeed, these courses should only be taken after sound primary studies, during which priority must be given to spiritual and moral values.
To prove the point I have just made, that education should be as sound as possible, but chiefly to give a spiritual and moral trend to our education, I shall quote from a speech made by Dr. Jean Spekkens, a professor of French at the University of Ottawa, about

the 20th of March, 1952, I believe, before the members of the Richelieu club of Ottawa. Dr. Spekkens, a Dutchman who came to Canada not quite six months ago in order to teach French at the University of Ottawa, said: "The danger resulting from the too rapid growth of industry is that the student is taught too much practical knowledge, while not enough interest is taken in his intellect."
Dr. Spekkens sums up his remarks by saying that, on the whole, the teachings and advice given to students should lean towards the elimination of materialism and the raising of intellectual standards.
Consequently, even if we have to consider the constitutional aspects of our educational problem, one must consider also the result which it may bring forth in the minds of our youth, so that when these young people succeed us in the management not only of public affairs, but particularly of social security, they may be in a position to give that general leadership which can make a people good and strong and lead it towards a philosophic and moral system consistent with our institutions as we see them today.
It is my understanding that a member from the province of Quebec, speaking on this subject of education tonight, is bound to at least express his opinion on the motion now under consideration, which I shall read once more:
-the government should take into consideration the advisability of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
If I am not mistaken, the general idea is that the provinces and the municipalities of the country need more money in order to devote greater amounts to education. Evidently, I am not in a position to know how critical the situation of the other provinces is: I am conversant only with the situation in my own province. My province benefits from the existence of a fund for education, a fund which is well-filled through the collecting of taxes which are supposed to be applied to education.
Under our federal system, the provinces are supposed to enjoy full autonomy in the important field of education. I think, and I suppose the majority of the members of this house share my view, that to act otherwise would be to sow seeds of discord among the population of our country and to endanger our nation itself.

The rights of the provinces are supreme in the field of education. The citizens of Canada ask but one thing, that the provincial authorities make an intelligent use of their rights and of their autonomy and that they keep politics out of that vital matter.
The word "education" should never be used to hide political motives. The money collected for education should never be used for any other government program, even though provincial authorities deem advisable to use the money for highway projects, as happened in the past. Should there be a surplus in the fund earmarked for education, let us give it to universities who need the money badly. I would like to quote an item from Le Devoir reproduced in Le Soleil of December 31, 1952. You will see what Le Devoir, which is an independent paper or, at least, is considered as such by the majority of the readers and of the people, has to say about the federal grants which were made last year and offered again this year to universities of the provinces. In quoting Le Devoir 'I do not believe that I am quoting a paper which gives its undivided support to the federal government.
To refuse such necessary assistance-
That is the grants which the federal government wants to give universities.
-would prejudice the very principle which we are seeking to uphold, i.e., autonomy in the field of education. If our universities were richly endowed -or if they had enough money to live instead of merely existing-the problem of federal aid might never have been raised. It is only after surveying the financial situation of the universities that the Massey commission asserted its conviction that the problem is one for the whole nation to consider. Had the universities not been so hungry, they undoubtedly would not have accepted, through sheer greediness, the gift offered by Ottawa. They would have repeated, "Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes". Because one may be justified to steal to save one's life so our universities accepted the money which they needed. To solve the financial problem of the universities would be to safeguard autonomy against coercion. By allowing it to subsist we might ward off centralization for a time but we make it inevitable, because poverty is a bad counsellor.
The same paper, speaking of the question of pupils and teachers, said this-and I am again quoting the August 21 issue of Le Soleil:
If the provincial state does not wish to see the colleges take federal subsidies, it must immediately revise its system of grants and adapt it to changing times. Colleges, like everybody else, need money; whether they be in charge of the laity or the clergy. The state will soon have to help them out to a far greater degree that it does now.
Education
The Sherbrooke Tribune speaks in the same vein of rural schools. There is much talk nowadays of the pressing need of municipalities for provincial or federal grants in aid of education. The Tribune then says this:
Rural schools, like large urban institutions, will soon be reopened. It so happens though that, in a large number of places, there is a shortage of teachers. This shortage would certainly not exist if, in certain rural districts, there was not such an attempt to scrimp and save on the remuneration of those who, by taste as well as by special training, formerly looked to a teaching career.
The Three Rivers Nouvelliste, which is read by a great many members, wrote:
Many who remained faithful to the career (the teaching profession) are only too willing to desert it for better paid employment. Teaching is often in the English provinces only a stepping stone. Thousands of examples could be mentioned. The situation is not quite so critical in the province of Quebec. That is due mostly to the contribution of the teaching orders. But even the teaching orders admit that they have not enough members to comply with all the requests which are made to them.
Therefore, there are two things to remember: our educational institutions-our universities, our colleges and our rural schools- need much more money to increase their contribution to education. Besides, if the federal government cannot, as they did last year, extend grants to universities; if the universities cannot, for reasons that I do not wish to discuss here, accept federal grants, then let it be said, as Le Devoir has done. If our purpose is to preserve autonomy by opposing all federal grants to universities, then let the provinces themselves consider larger financial help to the universities. Our provincial educational fund is quite large and, if and when a surplus exists, we could offer more to universities which thus would no longer be obliged to accept federal money.
Clearly, as a representative of the province of Quebec and as an out-and-out autonomist, I cannot vote in favour of this resolution, whereby we are asked "to equalize educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose."
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I believe in autonomy. My acts are in accordance with my words when I think of the autonomy of my province in the field of education, and if there is an autonomy which is to be respected, it is that one; if we want education to receive the grants it needs, let us be serious, so that the autonomy granted the provinces under our constitution may be well used, well felt; it should be considered and observed not through the glasses of politicians, but through those of citizens who really believe in provincial autonomy.

Education
We sometimes have some trouble; my French-speaking and Catholic compatriots sometimes have educational difficulties because of the provisions of our constitution. Tonight I shall not discuss the merits or demerits of certain claims made by my compatriots. The fact remains that they are in a difficult situation in certain districts as far as the teaching of French is concerned. That should not exist in a country like Canada. I believe it a fundamental principle that the taxpayer should have the right to enjoy whatever services are derived from the taxes he pays. Therefore, such a clause should be included in any declaration of human rights. We should also be determined to respect it and have it respected.
What purpose would there be in having a declaration of human rights, unless it embodies that fundamental principle, unless we are determined to enforce that fundamental right of the taxpayer to benefit from grants made by various governments. Such a situation should not be because the taxpayer has a right to his share. The province of Quebec gives a striking example of the fullest understanding of what should be an educational system in a province where there are rather marked ethnological differences.
A few years ago I quoted a statement from the secretary of the Protestant Board of Education of the province of Quebec, Mr. W. T. Percival, director of the Protestant schools in that province. He is reported by the Ensign as having said, on May 20, 1950, that education, in the province of Quebec, is just like a fairy tale. He was referring to the tolerance between Protestants and Catholics. He said that the development of Protestant schools in the province of Quebec could very well be likened to a fairy tale. Why is that so, Mr. Speaker? Because we respect the rights of minorities in the field of education and teaching. Therefore in a country such as ours our French-speaking citizens should really not have to press any claims with regard to their right to receive instruction in their own language and also to receive their part of grants in aid of education, whether their children go to public or denominational schools.
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that, when we have any claims to press, or when we are in some trouble, some of our compatriots give up. I do not really know what to think about all this, and I will pass no judgment. It is sad to hear them, sometimes, not only in the field of education, but also when we meet with certain difficulties from a financial or constitutional point of view.

The other day we heard a lecture given by one of my compatriots who said: Must the province of Quebec leave confederation? I do not think that the province of Quebec must leave confederation; that would be the end of Canada and of confederation.
I do not wish to speak too much or elaborate too much on this lapse on the part of one of our public men.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have here a striking example. When an army commander sees his army engaged in battle, no matter how serious the battle, no matter how numerous his enemies are, if he is courageous, he does not leave the battlefield, he does not ask his soldiers to leave the battlefield; on the contrary, he goes on fighting and, like Henry IV, he says: "Follow the plume of my helmet, it will always lead you to victory". This commander tells them not to leave the battlefield, but to go on fighting in order to achieve victory and "pour emporter le morceau" as we say in French.
The province of Quebec has been part of confederation since 1867. It has always played a leading role and it continues to do so. I would not like it to be said in any quarter that the French Canadians are quit-' ters, that the moment they meet with difficulties they are prone to say: We are going to secede from confederation.
Mr. Speaker, since 1867 this question of autonomy has always been discussed, and the province of Quebec has done so in the most objective way possible. We are still alive, we have kept our institutions, we speak, sing, discuss politics in French, and we speak English as well as French. We are still free. Since 1867, this question of autonomy has come up regularly.
Mr. Speaker, before speaking of autonomy we should begin by making good use of it. We should first know what it means. Tonight we are speaking of education, a matter that is closely connected with autonomy and in regard to which autonomists are always ready to uphold their rights.
Therefore, I cannot vote in favour of the motion, because I believe we should wait and see how the provinces will act, whether they will decide to accept federal grants to their universities, their colleges-grants to the educational fund as we say in my province. Let the provinces speak. It is not up to us to tell the provinces they should accept this or that arrangement. It is not up to us to tell them that we, in this house, have adopted a motion which would request the govern-

ment to distribute to our schools grants for educational purposes and see that these were properly apportioned. Consequently I am opposed to it. If there is one thing the people from the province of Quebec for the most part have no wish of doing it is to show signs of weakness by wanting to go their own way. If we have discussed the question, a thorny one admittedly, it is only because I and most of my compatriots do not fear to go forward. No, the province of Quebec entertains no thought of slacking. That is not her style, as she has always shown.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this motion will at least have one good effect. It will have enabled us to speak our minds clearly, fully, with no political reservations, to discuss objectively and ask our leaders in the province of Quebec to keep up the struggle from the point of view of autonomy, but on a higher plane. That is what this motion has allowed us to say in this house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on the resolution before us at this time, which envisages aid by the federal government to the provinces and therefore presumably would include aid in respect of education at all levels, from the secondary schools up to and including universities.
Although I could not follow the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) as well as I should have liked, I know he did cover educational problems at various levels, including those of the universities in his own province.
This afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) suggested that, in so far as the burden of education in respect of high schools and secondary schools is concerned, the cost must fall upon the municipalities and provinces, and that within the framework of the tax agreements the provinces will have to find the money with which to finance the necessary educational projects. In that connection I was struck by what is contained in the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics which, I have no doubt, was received by all hon. members this morning. Glancing over it, I saw on the first page this amazing statement, that the secondary school enrolment in Canada, exclusive of Quebec, is expected to double in the course of the next twelve years. In 1951 the number of students in the secondary schools of the nine provinces was 296,900. Last year it was 298,000. In 1953 it is expected to be from
Education
305,000 to 313,000, and in 1964 somewhere between 569,000 and 611,000.
If the bureau is correct in its estimate, and it usually is, we will see within the next few years a doubling of the school population in this country at the secondary school level.
I think every hon. member will admit that today municipalities and provinces are finding it most difficult to finance their present burdens. If the school population is to be doubled, how can they finance with the revenues now available to them?
I suggest that these figures in themselves show the absolute necessity for a reconsideration of this whole problem, and for intervention by the federal government to assist the provinces. I am not reiterating what was said today by my leader and others when I say that what I suggest would in no way impinge upon provincial autonomy. What is the use of provincial autonomy if the schools are so crowded, as they will be within the next few years, that they cannot provide the facilities with which to educate our children?
This is a time for vision, imagination and courage. Due to war conditions, increased marriages, heavy employment, and immigration policies, we are finding a tremendous increase in our population. Some means must be provided whereby this increased population can be served, and I suggest this resolution is one step in that direction.
I know that in my own province today teachers are not paid on the scale on which they should be paid, or a scale sufficient to attract the necessary number of men and women to that profession. Each one of them could earn more money in some other field. How can we have a strong and virile educational system when our school teachers do not earn as much money as mechanics or tradesmen who, entitled as they may be to a proper wage, do not have to spend the time required by teachers in acquiring professional knowledge, nor do they have to carry the same responsibilities. We must always keep in mind that we place the training of our youth upon the shoulders of our teachers. These are the statements we make so often and, while I do not wish to repeat old cliches, I do say it is time we did something more than repeat these statements. It is high time we did something to improve the situation.
In my province we pioneered in establishing the first free schools in this country. We blazed the trail in matters of education, and in many ways we are still doing it. I know one hon. member who now serves in this House of Commons who knows intimately the problems with which we in Nova Scotia are confronted. I say without hesitation that

Education
that problem cannot be solved unless we receive federal assistance at some level such as that proposed in the resolution.
I have already made reference to the grants to universities, and the basis of distribution of those grants. In that connection I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared the other day in the Halifax Herald. I do not propose to quote it at length but, inasmuch as other newspaper reports have been placed on the record to set out the educational problem, perhaps I might be permitted to quote briefly from this editorial. It says, in part:
As the days pass without a sign from the federal authorities, the anxiety of Nova Scotians over the distribution of federal aid for higher education naturally deepens. The fear is that, unless the authorities recognize the disparity which has existed and adopt a fairer system of distribution, our universities will have to operate for still another year with less assistance than those in other provinces.
And then it says:
Nova Scotian universities have not asked for special consideration, but merely for parity, for fair play.
Our universities are not subsidized by the state, but depend upon private support. In a relatively low-income area support should be forthcoming from the state, and those grants should be on a basis of a strict payment per student, rather than on a basis of 50 cents per head of population, as now obtains.
I dealt with this matter at some length on an earlier occasion and shall not go into it in detail now, more than to say that I hope when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduces his budget he will announce that a new system has been inaugurated whereby grants will be paid per head, per student, rather than on the basis of a certain amount per head of population as it is now. The method I suggest is the one that was followed by the government in financing the education of our veterans. I am sure it takes pride in its record in that regard, and I am sure, too, that the universities and students concerned found that it was a most satisfactory procedure.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear". I hope he will say that to the government, and see to it that it changes the basis upon which it is now operating, so that it may give aid to students in the manner I have indicated. Certainly if that is not done, then the least that must be done is to change the provincial basis under which we now operate and with which I dealt a little while ago. The universities just cannot carry on today with the moneys that are available to them,

nor can students go to university. I have figures here taken quickly from the Massey report which show the situation so far as students are concerned in both secondary schools and universities. That report, as many of us will remember, stated that out of every 100 students entering common school only 22 finish high school and only three graduate from college. The report goes on to say that of those who dropped out, 54 per cent did so for economic reasons. In other words these students could not afford to finish high school and go on to college. That is a situation to which attention should be paid.
When you look at another table in the Massey report you find that so far as colleges are concerned-I only have the figures which the report uses, from 1943 to 1949; I have not gone beyond that-the income of universities derived from students increased from 34-3 per cent to 48 per cent, and it was still increasing. You find that the income derived from endowment had fallen from 15-9 per cent to 8 per cent, and that the income from provincial governments by way of grants had fallen from 40 [DOT] 5 per cent to 32 per cent. Yet at the same time the amount the universities were paying out per student had decreased from $515 in 1943 to $433 in 1949. Despite the depreciated value of the dollar and the lost purchasing power, the actual dollars spent by universities per student had fallen from $515 to $433. So you have the amazing situation that the students were paying more, that their actual proportion had increased from 34-3 per cent to 48 per cent, yet they were receiving substantially less. The reason for that of course is that the universities just could not get the money elsewhere. They have been raising fees and raising fees until students can scarcely pay them.
That brings into focus one particular matter which I should like to mention, the reference in the Massey report to scholarships for students. That is one way the government can aid the educational system at the moment. We will remember that the Massey report urges the government to inaugurate a system of national scholarships whereby worthy students can receive aid and go on to university. If that happened it would reduce the load of the universities because their plant and equipment are there, and the more students they get the easier it is for them to operate. Such scholarships would go a long way toward solving, at least on a university level, the problem to which the resolution refers. It is a direct recommendation of that report, Mr. Speaker.
This is a matter which demands immediate attention. When you scan the figures I have

given showing increased costs you realize how difficult it is for students to continue with their education today. As we are entering educational week and the attention of the nation is focused on that, I would suggest and urge that the government carry out that recommendation and announce this spring a system of national scholarships for students throughout the nation.
Mr. Speaker, earlier in the day I was informed while in my office that some reference was made to me by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight).
Don't pay any attention.
At the time I was attending to certain matters of importance to some of my constituents, but I came down to the house to see what the-
Fuss.

-trouble was all about. I was not able then to read a transcript of the hon. member's speech, and by the time I entered the house he had passed the point in his remarks where he was alluding to me. I was not able to see a transcript until after supper. However, I have now given it a cursory examination and I think it requires an answer. I think he found it to be somewhat a matter of mirth that I did not take his motion exactly at its face value, and that I had perhaps suggested in other places that there might be some political intent in addition to the very fine spirit conveyed by the wording of the actual resolution.
I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) when he says that at some future time this very desirable resolution will likely be implemented, or that something will be done along this line. However, I have searched in vain in the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon and other members of his party for a solution to the problem and a way of making this most desirable motion effective. The only thing I have heard from any of these hon. gentlemen is that we should pass on some money from the federal treasury to the provincial governments and that they should be allowed to spend it without any supervision whatsoever.
I take issue with that, and I have certain reasons why I think it should be taken issue with. The principle of taxation without responsibility is not a very good one. The idea of asking the federal government to tax the people of the country and hand the money on to somebody else without any supervision of the spending is not a good thing whether the money is for education or something else.
Education
It has been suggested that we follow such a procedure in other cases, and that is quite correct. So far as health is concerned we hand money over without supervision, but education is something a little bit different. Education, particularly in the province of Quebec and in other parts of Canada as well, is very closely allied to religion. In fact I defy anybody to draw a distinct line between the two. In order to bring this matter to your attention a little more strongly, I should like to refer to an incident that occurred in my riding. I am trying to show why we cannot give money willy-nilly to the provinces. In my riding last year we had a teacher who was employed by the larger school unit as an extra teacher. He went around and filled in where teachers were absent from work for one reason or another. I was told by the parent of some children whom he went to teach one day, together with other children, in the town of Glenbush, that in the course of his remarks he told them there was no God, that they were wasting their time going to church, and that they could spend it much better in some other ways. Protests were made by the parents of these children, but apparently they were disregarded.
The point I wish to make is that if the federal government is going to tax the people of this country in order to be able to hand money over to a province which cares not whether that type of thing is taught to children in our schools, then I think the people who are paying federal taxes will rise up in arms before they will allow a thing of that kind.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) said he found some enjoyment in the fact that I had mentioned that I thought there was some political intent. Possibly we have not his developed sense of humour, but I gather that there was not any great applause or show of humour in this house at that remark. I would suggest that possibly the C.C.F. party is amenable to that idea, that that kind of thing should be taught in the schools. If they can show me otherwise; if they can show me any possible way this very desirable motion can be put into effect, I will be very pleased to support it; but I cannot support the idea that we pass money along to any province without some safeguards. I think the object lesson I have just quoted is a good case in point to show why we should not.
I might also add, concerning the particular remarks I mentioned, that the parent told me that the gentleman mentioned made a mockery of religion and a mockery of church with these children. The parent said his

Education
children were quite put out about it and so was he; and I do not blame him in the least.
With respect to the other allegation the hon. member for Saskatoon put on record this afternoon, I think perhaps I can find some further support. Certainly I am not the only person who thinks there might be some political intent. Just recently we have had some outbursts from the premier of Quebec, a gentleman who might have considerable to say before any changes are made in our educational set-up. Mr. Duplessis says:
Education has guaranteed survival of Quebec's religion and language traditions and could never be surrendered.
That is fairly emphatic. Another headline reads:
Duplessis says "Encroachments" question of "Life and Death".
Well, I think he has his eye on the motion of the hon. member when he says that; and I just wonder whether the hon. member for Saskatoon does not himself subscribe to the idea proposed by the school teacher in Glen-bush. Some weight might be lent to the suggestion that he does, because I have here a report from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix which says that the hon. member for Saskatoon went to the town of Meadow Lake and asked the people there to support that gentleman in the forthcoming election and elect him to this house. That would lend some support to the idea that possibly the hon. member for Saskatoon supports that gentleman's ideas. He at least supports him, although the latter is an avowed atheist. He picks this gentleman, or his convention does, and he immediately supports him and tells the people of Meadow Lake that he is the man they should send to this house.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
You may ask it.

First of all, has my hon. friend any evidence that this particular occurrence took place in the school, or is it merely gossip or hearsay? Secondly, has he any evidence to show that I have any acquaintance with the gentleman who was nominated and any acquaintance with his religious or other opinions?

I have no evidence that the hon. member knows what his religious beliefs are, but I have evidence here to show that the hon. member went to Meadow Lake to support the gentleman; and having been very closely allied-

Mr. Speaker, on a point of privilege, the hon. gentleman is basing his

whole case on hearsay. In the first place he says that some gentleman was nominated-
That is not privilege.
-at Meadow Lake. According to hearsay he told children somewhere that there was no God, or he made some other irreligious statement.
What is the question?

My hon. friend presumes I knew of that, and he said that in spite of it I supported the gentleman. My only contact with him was because there was a convention there and I went to make the main speech in the evening after the people of Meadow Lake, constituents of my hon. friend, nominated their candidate. I have no idea of his religious views, any more than I have about the religious opinions of my hon. friend.
Tell them what you said about the maritimes.
I could tell you lots of hearsay and gossip but I would not think of doing so. I would not stoop to it.
The hon. gentleman wanted to know the name of the gentleman who was nominated. If he does not know who was nominated there, he should.
I don't want the name, I want evidence.
I want to make this speech now, and you can make yours tomorrow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is not a speech, it is just gossip.
Tell us what he said about the maritimes.

I want to explain again some of the humour of the member for Saskatoon. Here is an idea of it from a headline in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
Knight says maritimes fear-ridden.
Residents of the maritime provinces do not enjoy the right of free speech, according to R. R. Knight, C.C.F. member for parliament for Saskatoon.
Speaking at a public meeting of the Saskatchewan branch of the C.C.F.-
"I think in Saskatchewan today we are the freest people on the North American continent," declared Mr. Knight. "When I think of the state of political fear in which many people in eastern Canada live, I am thankful that I live in the west."
We are thankful he lives there too.

It goes on:
-on many occasions-people would like to go to the C.C.F. meetings but the night is not dark enough-
The night is not dark enough for us to listen to him.

That is some of the hon. gentleman's humour.
To deal somewhat one-sidedly with another matter with which he dealt-and it cannot be otherwise because he was a spectator on the sidelines-I will refer to a letter that was sent to me last year by the Saskatchewan school trustees association. I will also mention the very fine deal the hon. member said the Meadow Lake riding was getting in the way of educational grants from the provincial government. I think the hon. member for Saskatoon said we were getting 72 per cent of our educational cost from the provincial government. If those figures are correct there is some reason to question why the people of the town of Meadow Lake are called upon to pay 42 mills for educational purposes, while in the surrounding area they pay 38 mills on agricultural lands. Those are correct figures because I got them from a member of the larger unit board.
However, to put the record straight I will deal with the letter which the hon. gentleman quoted this afternoon. He said that 20 members of parliament had been sent this letter, and when I said I was waiting for my copy he could not understand it. The Saskatchewan school trustees association could not understand it either, and they know a lot more about it than the hon. member. I know a lot more about it, too, and I am the only one in possession of all the facts because the letter finally reached me and I know how it came here. The letter that he put on Hansard was dated March 25 at Regina. Oddly enough it reached here on March 24, a day ahead of the day it was written.
An advance copy.

This particular letter, Mr. Speaker, asked me to apologize in the house for something I had not said; and I think the school trustees association are convinced of that now. I wrote to them and cleared the record on it. I gave them chapter and verse, and so far all I have had from them is a very nice letter from the secretary saying he had received it, and taking no issue with it whatsoever. So I can take it from that, I think, that my letter was fairly correct.
The main reason that I did not get my copy of the letter was that they sent the other 19 Saskatchewan members' letters to the House of Commons. We were sitting at that time, and I had allegedly made this speech to which they took exception. My copy of the letter was sent to Meadow Lake, a place in which I do not live even when I am home. This letter went to Meadow Lake and then to Medstead, where I do live. It was then forwarded to the House of Commons, but by then I had gone
Education
home for the Easter recess so it followed me on to Medstead. I finally got this letter, which is dated March 25, 1952, on April 15.
I believe I covered the points fully in my reply to this letter. Since the hon. gentleman has put the other letter on the record, perhaps I had better read this reply into the record. It is addressed to Mr. Z. M. Hamilton, secretary treasurer, Saskatchewan school trustees association, and it reads:
Your letter of March 25 with copy of your press release of March 22, finally reached me on the 15th of April. A glance at your copy will immediately show the reason for the delay in its reaching me. Similar letters sent on the same day by your office to 19 Saskatchewan members were received here on the 24th of March, a day before they were officially written. In every one of these 19 cases they were addressed to the House of Commons- for some reason, best known to your office, mine was dispatched to the town of Meadow Lake-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They think you should not be here.

I am omitting some of the parts because this letter is lengthy.
After reading your press release here in the house on March 24, I waited patiently for your letter for a couple of weeks before I made any statement, as I did not want to be guilty of the same offence which you committed, namely, discussing something that I had never seen. At that time, however, seeing no letter had arrived, it was necessary for me to put the record straight in view of your hasty and incorrect conclusions drawn in your press release. Had you read my speech first, I have no doubt but that you would never have put out the press release that you did, because nowhere in my speech can you find anything, either directly or implied, as even remotely suggesting that the school trustees association had anything to do with the 1,558 schools either closed or without qualified teachers in Saskatchewan. I was attacking provincial government policy, and provincial government policy only, which basically was the inability of school boards to go out and bid for qualified teachers' services-in other words, by placing ceilings on the wages of various classes of teachers, they had short-circuited the system of "supply and demand" to the end that in six years time we had 558 school rooms open, which were without a qualified teacher, but instead, a sitter.
As a school trustees association, you are quite likely familiar with the conducting and marking of efficiency contests. In the light of this I would like you to assess the press release that was carried so unanimously by your executive meeting. The first essential in criticizing anyone or anything is to properly identify them so that people will know who or what you are talking about. The first thing your press report does is to identify one J. L. Harrison, as M.P. for Meadow Lake. No such man has ever sat for Meadow Lake or any other constituency in Canada since confederation. I trust that you will say that this is a typographical error. It is still an error, and error No. 1. Error number two, is your statement that my speech was false and malicious, causing great injustice to school trustees and teachers in Saskatchewan. As school trustees were never mentioned, and the only thing I suggested about teachers was that boards be allowed to compete for their services on a market of short supply, it is hard to imagine how anyone could construe this

Education
as being one detrimental to the teachers. Your third error is that. "Mr. Harrison is ignorant of the true situation of education in Saskatchewan and the benefits obtained by his home town of Meadow Lake". Meadow Lake is not my home town, but is 85 miles away from it. This you will also wish to claim as an error, and I am prepared to allow it as such. Assuming that Meadow Lake is my home town, however, as you do, the fourth error still remains, that I am ignorant of the benefits obtained by Meadow Lake. Let's just see who is ignorant here, or whether we both have the same understanding of the word "benefits". Certainly the people of Meadow Lake are not aware of these benefits; and far from being ignorant of the situation, I took the trouble to inquire, as late as February before coming down here, from a member of the larger unit board, as to the status quo in Meadow Lake, and got the following information: The town of Meadow Lake has a mill rate for school purposes only, of 42 mills. If this is beneficial, those members of your executive who are so unanimous about everything, should make it their business to go to Meadow Lake and explain it to the people there. For my part, I defy you to find any town in Canada outside the borders of Saskatchewan, that has a mill rate even approaching 42 mills for school assessment only. I was further informed by this member of the larger unit, that the surrounding hamlets were assessed at the rate of 40 mills for school purposes; and something which no one outside of Saskatchewan can believe, is that farm property owners are assessed 38 mills for school purposes. If you knew of these figures when you talked so glibly in the press of the beneficial situation existing in Meadow Lake, then you have a very different idea of what the word "beneficial" means, than I have. If you are going to tell me now that you did not know of these figures, then my question immediately is, who is really ignorant about the situation at Meadow Lake, myself, as you claim in the press, or your association? I think you had better justify the figures to the people of Meadow Lake or admit that you are ignorant of the situation. The fifth, and I think the worst error is, publicizing the fact all over the country that you are writing all Saskatchewan members of the House of Commons, including myself, asking me to apologize for something I have never said, and then shipping my letter off to Meadow Lake. I do not think that you would want to tell me that you did this intentionally, and I do not think you did, myself. The most charitable view of it that can be taken is, that it was another error.
If the foregoing had been entered in one of your efficiency contests, I have no doubt it would get a rating of zero. If not, I would be interested to learn what standards you use.
I am always quite ready to render apologies when I have mistakenly wronged someone, and I don't have to do that very often. Frankly, however, on the record, I ask you, who should apologize to who? If you are fair, your answer will be clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but it is not usually in order to read into the record such long quotations. I think the hon. member should perhaps give the general tenor of the arguments contained in that letter or document, and not put the whole of the document on Hansard.

The first letter, to which this is a reply, was placed on the record in its
entirety. Possibly there are some parts of this letter that I could skip, and quote the concluding paragraph. I am putting the letter on the record to keep the record straight, as it should be if the matter is to be discussed at all. I believe my hon. friends will agree with that. I shall quote the concluding paragraph:
In all the foregoing, sir, nothing is aimed at you personally, as I am quite aware that you are a hired secretary, and therefore have to do what you are told.
The letter finishes on that line of thought. He replies as follows:
I would like, at this time, to express to you my appreciation of the last paragraph of your letter where personal reference has been made to myself.
I believe that clears up the matter so far as we are concerned. The matter of federal aid is something which, on its face and as put on the order paper by the hon. member, is desirable. As soon as my hon. friends across the way will introduce some system of making it effective, other than just handing money over for someone to run around the country and preach atheism, I shall be glad to support the measure.
That letter is proof that we need federal aid.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we will consider the following measures: First, the motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister relating to Mondays and Wednesdays; then the motion in the name of the Minister of National Revenue concerning the setting up of a committee on broadcasting; then third reading of Bill No. 45; then the resolution in the name of the Postmaster General to amend the Post Office Act; Bill No. 103, to amend the National Defence Act; Bill No. 102, respecting the royal style and titles; Bill No. 105, respecting the liability of the crown for torts and civil salvage; Bill No. 38, respecting the Saint John Bridge and Railway Extension Company; Bill No. 19, to amend the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act. These are small bills.
Then we shall take up Bill No. 39, to amend the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act; Bill No. 40, respecting the appointment of auditors for national railways. If we have time left, we shall take up Bill No. 44, to protect the coastal fisheries.
You may bring in the budget after eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Are we to be dissolved tomorrow night?
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, January 27, 1953
